en: Preface to the Commentary on the *Vajrasamādhi Sūtra*:
The true mind alone is revealed, like the bright moon shining in the vast void; the Dharma-nature is without deficiency, like a black pearl radiating from the blue sea.
It is clearly manifest and never obscured in daily life, luminously present and unborn even within birth—this is True Suchness (*tathatā*).

Not abiding in its own nature, it manifests and arises according to conditions; yet this arising is non-arising. Because the true mark (*dharmatā*) is originally devoid of things, not even a single speck of dust is received;
though one seeks it, it cannot be found. It is like fire within wood: it is certainly present, yet there is no fixed location to rely upon.

To realize its essence is to encounter the spirit (*śen*). It is comparable to a flower in a mirror: it is clearly visible, yet though one tries to grasp it, it cannot be obtained. It is non-existent.
Its wondrous function is like a mani-jewel reflecting colors: though the shadows shift, its essence remains truly unchanged.
It is fully present from the beginning, yet we are like impoverished sons who have strayed from their own homes; though our bodies suffer hardship, the treasure has never been absent. Alas!

We have been submerged for kalpas, our delusion and estrangement deepening further and further. The family wealth exists within us, yet it becomes difficult to recognize because we have not encountered a virtuous friend.
"Friend, from what source did you attain enlightenment? Therefore, I, the Tathāgata, departed from Tuṣita Heaven and descended to the Imperial Palace;

renouncing wealth and status, I fled to the Snowy Peaks and practiced austerities for six years. Upon beholding the stars, I attained the Way and became the compassionate father of all sentient beings and the preeminent teacher of the nine realms.

After thirty-seven days of contemplation, I turned the Great Wheel of Dharma; because the capacities of beings are difficult to harmonize—some being sharp and others dull—the teachings were thus divided into gradual stages."

For over forty years, though he desired to speak, he could not; the provisional and the ultimate obscured one another. Now that the time for *nirvāṇa* draws near, though he desires to cease, he cannot.
He exhaustively reveals the single mind, as if grasping a vajra sword to sever all doubts.

He erects the banner of the True Dharma to shatter all heterodox delusions, transforming the *hīnayāna* so that they purely enter the One Vehicle, and uniting the hundred rivers so they return to the same ocean.
The Ocean of Truth is the excellent medicine for saving the sick; it employs the precious raft to ferry humanity across.

Therefore, the World-Honored One, without being questioned, spoke of his own accord, bestowing ambrosia to universally rescue those suffering from chronic ailments. He recited gāthās to praise and extol, and as they sat together playing the lute, he caused them to attain liberation.
Having initiated this broad inquiry, he knew that the six pāramitās all return to the Mind-King of Non-Form. Thus he asked.
The meaning of non-arising is realized through the three practices as being solely one’s own mind; by demonstrating that there is no abiding, the Dharmakāya is revealed as neither coming nor going.

Through great power, the fruit and virtue are awakened; there is both realization and cultivation. Upon hearing the cause and conditions of this single verse, Śāriputra attained access to the true void, which fully encompasses the four virtues.
By maintaining the true practice of Brahma-conduct, one attains the single flavor; thus, within the conventional truth, the four conditions are suddenly perfected.
Ksitigarbha resolved the lingering doubts of the remaining seven chapters; Ānanda requested the title and the beginning and end of this single sutra.

From start to finish, it is nothing other than the clarification of one’s own mind throughout its preceding and succeeding states—how could it ever escape the nature of reality (*dharmatā*)? Alas, in this degenerate age, such a wondrous scripture is difficult to encounter.

Now that we have obtained this flawless work, which was bestowed through the Master Wuxia’s dream and divine inspiration, it is carved for circulation. Its purport is profound and its phrasing extraordinary; those who read it will surely find it so.
Thus, as if prompted by this, I, a person of humble and ignorant capacity, venture to extend my narrow vision.

While I, like those ancients, am not one who could cause a single word to ring like gold when cast upon the ground, nor one whose single utterance would pervade the great trichiliocosm, I nonetheless dare not claim such prowess;

yet, out of a heart that admires the Mahāyāna, I merely hope to offer praise. Since the words of the Sage are unfathomable and the intellect of ordinary beings is incapable of fathoming them, should there be any errors herein, I pray you will grant me absolution through repentance.

*Huǐmíng Chuán Cáo Dōng Zhèngzōng Dì Èrshíkqīdài Huìjī Yúnménshān Xiǎnshèngsì Zhùzhí Yuánchéng Zhù bìng Xù* (The Commentary and Preface by Yuánchéng, Abbot of Xiǎnshèng Temple on Mount Yúnmén in Huìjī,
the Twenty-seventh Generation of the Authentic Lineage of the Caodòng School, Transmitted by Huǐmíng).

First Fascicle of the Commentary on the *Vajrasamādhi-sūtra*.
Translator’s name lost; appended to the Northern Liang Record.
Annotated by the Śramaṇa Yuǎnchéng of Xiǎnshèng Monastery in Kuàijī.
Regarding the meaning of the *Vajra-samādhi*: it is translated as "Right View" (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*). In the world, "obscuration" (*maiti*) refers to not seeing;

in the Buddha-dharma, "right view" refers to non-seeing. Therefore, it is also called "Right Concentration" (*samyak-samādhi*), because it arises from the two practices [of wisdom and concentration] and thus exists.

The second is called "stopping" (*śamatha*); that which is produced by stopping is called "right concentration" (*samyak-samādhi*), while that which is produced by the cultivation of insight (*vipaśyanā*) is called "right view" (*samyak-dṛṣṭi*).
View expels internal delusions, while concentration repels external demons. Both together attain a firmness that is likened to the vajra.
Now, as for the meaning of "vajra," there are many types; I shall briefly cite three names: the first is "that which can sustain. Second... [text continues].

First is vigor; second is strength; third is majesty. These three combined constitute that which can sustain the three worlds, for the "receptacle world" (bhājana-loka) is precisely that which is sustained.
Thus, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "Firm clarity establishes obstruction; firm awareness achieves the precious [substance]. Therefore, there is a golden wheel that maintains the land.
For this reason, all worlds depend upon the adamantine foundation (*vajra-pṛthivī*) for their support. As for "vigor":
This refers to the world of sentient beings; thus, among humans, there is the title "Vajra-wielding Malla.
Because his majestic power is that of the world of the Wisdom-Perfectly-Awakened One, he is called the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha-rāja.

With a concentrated mind, he swiftly subdues demonic adversaries and protects the patience of the Dharma. Know that whether they be sages or commoners, sentient or non-sentient, there are none who do not [fall under his influence].
All receive the Vajra-samādhi as the fundamental essence of original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*). Furthermore, it penetrates both cause and fruit;
since the cause is precisely the original enlightenment of sentient beings, it is said that "all sentient beings possess the root-faculty of original enlightenment.
This is why it is stated that "the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction. The fruit is precisely the initial enlightenment (*ādi-bodhi*) of all Buddhas.

This refers to the Bodhisattva awakening upon a lotus pedestal, receiving his office as all Buddhas of the ten directions simultaneously emit precious light to consecrate the crown of his head, whereby he enters the Vajra-samādhi and attains perfect enlightenment in a single kṣaṇa. One might ask:

"If the Vajra-samādhi is identical to the original enlightenment (prakṛti-bodhi) of sentient beings, why do they not all attain Buddhahood at once, such that there would be no distinction between ordinary beings and sages?"
What is the distinction? The answer is: regarding the Buddha-nature as the direct cause (*dharmatā-hetu*), the essence of the Buddha and that of sentient beings are fundamentally identical.

Regarding the Buddha-nature as the conditional cause (*pratyaya-hetu*), sentient beings have not yet fully possessed it; whereas all Bodhisattvas, by means of the ten faiths, ten abidings, ten practices, ten transferences, the ten stages (*bhūmi*), and the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), attain awakening upon reaching the stage of Equal Enlightenment.
It is only then that they obtain the Vajra-mind, beginning from the initial Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā-bhūmi*).

Thus, through these successive layers of single and double [teachings], the twelve [periods] are exhausted; yet because sentient beings lack the causal conditions for the wondrous enlightenment, they cannot all simultaneously attain Buddhahood.

Indeed, the Original Teacher, deeply knowing that all sentient beings are inherently complete from the beginning but remain deluded and fail to return [to their source), appeared in the world to guide and instruct sentient beings through various skillful means and various causes and conditions.

Knowing that one gradually cultivates and accumulates [wholesome qualities] based on conditions and causes until finally attaining what was previously non-existent is called "initial awakening" (*ādikṣaya-bodhi*).

The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* employs various metaphors; it says: "For example, wherever a diamond (*vajra*) is applied, there is nothing it does not shatter or destroy, yet the diamond itself suffers no fracture or loss.
The diamond-like samādhi (*vajropama-samādhi*) is also like this: wherever it is applied..."
There is no dharma that is not shattered and destroyed, yet this samādhi suffers no diminution.
Good son, just as the diamond is the most supreme among all jewels, so too is the diamond-like samādhi attained by the bodhisattva the foremost among all samādhis.
Why is this? Because the bodhisattva-mahāsattva cultivates this samādhi.
"O son of good family, all samādhis come to take refuge in and submit to this [Vajra-samādhi], just as all minor kings come to take refuge in and submit to a universal monarch (cakravartin).
All samādhis are likewise thus; they all come to take refuge in and submit to the Vajra-samādhi.
O son of good family, it is like a person who is hated and oppressed by enemies of the state, and another person kills him."
Just as all people in the world praise the merits of such a person, so too is the Vajra-samādhi;
when a bodhisattva cultivates it, they are able to destroy all enemies among sentient beings, and for this reason, it is always revered by all samādhis.
Good son, it is like a man whose strength is robust and powerful.
If there were someone who could further subdue those who are unsubduable, one should know that such a person is what the world calls "gold.
The Diamond Samādhi (*vajrasamādhi*) is also like this: it possesses the power to crush and subdue dharmas that are otherwise difficult to subdue.
For this reason, all samādhis come to take refuge and submit to it. Good son, it is as if there were a person in the great ocean.
One should know that such a person has already used the waters of all rivers, springs, and ponds;
likewise, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices this Vajra-samādhi should be known as having already practiced all other samādhis.
Good son, it is like a spring in the Fragrant Mountains named Anavatapta.
That spring is endowed with water of eight excellent qualities; whoever drinks it is free from all suffering and illness. The Vajra-samādhi is likewise thus:
it is endowed with the Eightfold Noble Path, and when Bodhisattvas cultivate it, they sever all afflictions, which are like festering sores and grave illnesses.
Good son, you should know that if a person makes offerings to Maheśvara, such a person has already [attained...]
The offering to all devas and the *vajrasamādhi* are likewise so.
If there is a person who practices this, one should know that they have already practiced all other samādhis.
Son of good family, if a bodhisattva dwells in this *vajrasamādhi*, they will see all phenomena without obstruction, as if [viewing] them within the palm of their hand.
In the contemplation of the *āmalaka* fruit, although the Bodhisattva attains such a vision, he ultimately does not form the conceptualization of seeing all phenomena.
Good son, it is like a person sitting at a crossroads who sees various sentient beings coming and going, sitting and lying down;
the Vajra-samādhi is also like this, seeing all phenomena arising and ceasing, appearing and disappearing. Well done!
Good son, it is like a high mountain: when a person ascends it and gazes afar in all directions, everything is clearly perceived.
The mountain of the diamond-like samādhi is also like this; when a bodhisattva ascends it and gazes afar at all phenomena, there is nothing that is not clearly perceived.
Good son, it is like the sweet rain sent down by the heavens during the spring months: its drops are so fine and dense that there is no space between them.
Just as one with pure eyes sees clearly, so too does the Bodhisattva;

having attained the pure eye of the Vajra-samādhi, they see all worlds in the eastern direction from afar—whether those lands are forming or decaying—and perceive them all clearly and without obstruction.
This is likewise true for the ten directions. O son of good family, it is like this: by means of...
When Mount Gandhamādana is struck by seven suns simultaneously, all its trees, groves, and forests are completely incinerated;
likewise, when a bodhisattva practices the Vajrasamādhi, all the thickets of afflictions are instantly extinguished.
Son of good family, for example, although a vajra is able to shatter all existing things...
Objects ultimately do not give rise to the thought, "I am able to destroy them. The diamond-like samādhi (*vajrasamādhi*) is also like this:
once a bodhisattva has cultivated it, they are able to destroy afflictions, yet they never give rise to the thought, "I am able to destroy the fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Good son, it is like the great earth, which can support all things, yet never gives rise to the thought, "My power is able to support them," nor does it think, "I [am supporting them]."
Fire does not think, "I can burn things"; water also does not think, "I can moisten and soak"; wind also does not think, "I can move things";
space also does not think, "I can provide room and containment"; and even Nirvāṇa likewise does not give rise to the thought, "I cause sentient beings to attain liberation.
The Vajrasamādhi is also like this: although it can eliminate all [defilements], it has no such thoughts.
Regarding afflictions, from the very beginning there is no thought or speech that "I can extinguish them.

If a bodhisattva dwells in such a vajra-samādhi, within a single thought-moment they manifest bodies like those of a Buddha, immeasurable in number and filling the worlds of the Buddhas throughout the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Although such a bodhisattva performs these transformations, their mind from the beginning...
He is free from thoughts of pride. Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva constantly reflects:
"Who possesses such concentration that they can perform such transformations? Only a Bodhisattva dwelling in this Vajra-samādhi is able to do so.
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in this Vajra-samādhi, in a single thought-moment he reaches everywhere throughout the ten directions.
Although he possesses the power to return Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges to their original places, he does not think, "I am able to do such a thing.
Why is this? It is because of the power of the causal conditions of this samādhi;
by dwelling in this Vajra Samādhi, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, in a single thought-moment, can sever [the afflictions] of the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Regarding all the afflictions of sentient beings in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, the Bodhisattva’s mind never initially conceives the thought of severing those afflictions.

Why is this? It is because by the power of the causal conditions of this samādhi, when a Bodhisattva abides in this Vajra-samādhi and expounds the Dharma with a single voice, all sentient beings each understand it according to their own kind.
By means of analogy, one attains understanding: it is manifested that while all sentient beings each see various forms and appearances, they all abide in a single place without their bodies shifting;
yet, according to the directions from which they face, each sentient being sees [the Buddha] differently.
Thus, when a single Dharma—whether it be the *dhātus* or the *āyatanas*—is expounded, all sentient beings each perceive it according to their own fundamental capacity for understanding.
Having attained this, the Bodhisattva dwells securely in such a samādhi that although he perceives sentient beings, his mind from the outset has no perception of the mark of a sentient being;
although he perceives men and women, there is no mark of man or woman; although he perceives form-dharmas, there is no mark of form;
even when perceiving consciousness, there is no mark of consciousness; and although he perceives day and night, there is no mark of day or night. Furthermore—
One sees all things, yet there is no sign of anything; though one sees all afflictions and fetters, there is no sign of any affliction.
One sees entry into the noble path, yet there is no sign of a noble path; though one sees enlightenment, there is no sign of enlightenment;
one sees nirvana, yet there is no sign of nirvana. Why is this? O son of good family, because all dharmas are [empty of intrinsic nature].
Because they are fundamentally without marks, the Bodhisattva, by the power of this samādhi, perceives all dharmas as being fundamentally without marks.
For what reason is it called the Vajra Samādhi? Good son, for example, if a vajra is placed in the sunlight, its color is not fixed;
the Vajra Samādhi is also like this—when it is among a great assembly, its appearance is likewise [not fixed].
Because it is indeterminate, it is called the Vajra Samādhi.
Son of good family, for example, just as no person in the world can appraise the value of a vajra, so too is the Vajra Samādhi;
all its merits cannot be measured by any among gods or humans. For this reason, it is further named the Vajra Samādhi. Son of good family, for example...
Just as a poor person who obtains a vajra-jewel immediately becomes free from poverty, suffering, malevolent spirits, and evil poisons, so too it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva:
upon attaining this samādhi, they are able to remain far removed from the afflictions, all sufferings, and the evil poisons of the Māras.
For this reason, it is further named the Vajra Samādhi; thus one knows the Vajra Samādhi.
The meaning and benefit are profound, and its inconceivable merit is beyond thought; how could it be discussed by those of limited wisdom?

Following the Great Master Tiantai’s method of using the fivefold profound meaning (*pañcavidha-gambhīrārtha*) to explain the purport of a single sutra, this scripture is designated by three names that together refer to one sutra:
first, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-sūtra*, which refers to that which encompasses; second, the *Vajra*... [the third name follows].
Obscurity is precisely the Dharma; the third is called the Principle of Immeasurable Meanings (*Ananta-artha*).

This refers to the signless Dharmakāya, which is the fundamental principle for all phenomena—this is the meaning of the Middle Way. Liberation is fierce and sharp, crushing the solid and destroying delusions—this is the meaning of Wondrous Existence (*Pratītyasamutpāda*).
Prajñā is without cognition yet knows nothing it does not know, universally containing all existence—this is the meaning of True Emptiness (*Śūnyatā*). This is the progression [of the teachings].
It does not reach the four stages of falling back, nor does it reach the two stages of *śaikṣa*; thus, these three names are established.
One should know that this sutra is titled according to the perfect fusion of the three virtues (*triguṇa*), manifesting the secret treasury (*guhyagarbha*) and acting as the precursor to *nirvāṇa*.
Question: Since it possesses all three names, why is it specifically named the *Vajrasamādhi*? Answer: It is so named because the meaning of "shattering delusions" (*moha-bheda*) is most prominent.

Because its essence consists of the beneficial activity of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-āveṇika-bodhi*), the title at the beginning of this sutra is "The Single Flavor, True Reality, Signless, Unborn, Determinate Ultimate Reality of Original Enlightenment's Beneficial Activity.
If there are those who hear this sutra, or even receive and uphold a single four-line verse from it, such persons shall enter the stage of the Buddha’s wisdom.
Since its central tenet is the true reality of ultimate emptiness, the verse says:
The single flavor is signless and its benefit is like the great void, which has nothing it cannot contain (and so forth).
Other sutras take the refutation of doubt and the sweeping away of attachment as their function; this sutra is not so.

Since there is no attachment to be swept away and no doubt to be refuted, taking non-transformation as transformation, non-cultivation as cultivation, and non-attainment as attainment—this is the wondrous function of this sutra.

Therefore, the Sūtra says: "If one transforms sentient beings without generating [the thought of] transforming them, and without generating [the thought of] non-transformation, that transformation is truly great" (and so forth).
While other sūtras take the individual excellence of their own specific flavor as their pedagogical characteristic (*śāsana-lakṣaṇa*), this sūtra is not like that;
it must be the *Prajñāpāramitā* or the final *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Why should it first take the two periods of time as indeterminate as its pedagogical characteristic? Regarding the *Prajñā*...
Although he was pointed toward his family’s wealth, he did not yet dare harbor the intention of seeking even a single meal; he remained outside the gate, lodging in a thatched hut.
Since he had not yet clearly realized the father-son relationship and remained ignorant of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), this sūtra verse states:
"One should preach the entry into reality for them, as all are in accordance with the One Vehicle," and further: "The Dharma of a single flavor moistens and fills everywhere."
Furthermore, since it definitively severs doubt and regret regarding all phenomena through the seal of a single dharma, could this not be considered the successor to the *Prajñāpāramitā*?

Although this sutra reveals the One Vehicle, the single dharma, the single rain, and the single flavor, because it has not yet received the direct transmission of the names of the kalpa, the land, and the auspicious title [of the Buddha], we know it precedes the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. If one follows the perspective of Xianshou, it is precisely the One Vehicle.
In other sutras of the Sudden Teaching, one practices through gradual cultivation until reaching the stage of Equal Enlightenment;

only then does awakening begin, and one attains the Vajra Mind at the initial stage of Dry Wisdom (*khaṇḍa-jñāna-bhūmi*). This sutra, however, before the assembly of devas and humans, suddenly proclaims the Vajra Samādhi without distinction between ordinary beings and sages.
When the great assembly attains awakening in a single thought-moment, it is called "the sudden realization of what was originally attained."
That this shares the same essence as the Buddha’s body is to know it as the Sudden Teaching (*dun-jiao*). "Sūtra" means the Way (*mārga*);
it is like the Great King’s highway, which all people may traverse together, without detours or deviations, bypassing all dangers and difficulties to reach the imperial capital directly.
This sūtra is likewise direct, abandoning expedient means to cause entry into the Buddha-way; it points directly to one's own mind, so that by seeing its nature, one achieves realization.
The Buddha does not fall into views or afflictions, nor does he engage with heterodox or Hinayana teachings; his truth is like the great highway to Chang’an.
Chapter One: Introduction.
Thus have I heard: At one time the Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain in the great city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of...
The assembly of the Bhagavat numbered ten thousand, all of whom had attained the path of Arhatship;

their names were Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Subhūti, and so forth. Among these Arhats, there were also two thousand Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, whose names were Liberation Bodhisattva, Mind-King Bodhisattva, Non-Abiding Bodhisattva, and so forth.
Furthermore, there were eighty thousand householders accompanying the Bodhisattvas, including the householder Brahmācārin,
the householder Mahābrahmā, the householder Jyotiṣka, and others such as these; additionally, there were six hundred thousand [beings],
including devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans.
"Oṃ. Such is the term used to point toward the Dharma. That which I have heard is the Dharma that possesses a basis of reliance; it is not a collection of errors gathered at a single time.
Because there are many different versions extensively cited, they are collectively referred to as consisting of five periods, namely: the period of the *Avataṃsaka*.
Regarding this sūtra, as clarified previously, it lies between the *Prajñāpāramitā* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
The Buddha is the master who expounds the Dharma, and Gṛdhrakūṭa is the place where the Dharma is propagated.

It is said that "I have heard such a Dharma from the Buddha" because one must know at what time and in what place the Buddha spoke it; thus, both time and place are mentioned together for this reason.
The general outline of the phenomenal aspects is thus; however, if one relies on the sequence of principle, it is not so. Why is this?

It is because the ultimate truth is without trace, without characteristic, and without form; it cannot be sought through words and letters, cannot be attained through existence or non-existence, cannot be borne by verbal expressions, and cannot be discerned by the mind or consciousness.
All such [conceptual] prohibitions are simply set aside, and it is merely called "thus" (tathatā).
This is merely to cause people to silently comprehend beyond the external and clearly discern before words.

Ānanda, fearing that people would not believe and might suspect this to be erroneous talk, pointed to the Buddha as his witness so that people would certainly believe it. Thus, the *Treasure Mirror Samādhi* says:
"Such a Dharma was secretly transmitted by the Buddhas and Patriarchs; now that you have obtained it, you should protect it well, like a silver bowl."
Amidst the gathering snow and the bright moon, the hidden and the revealed are not uniform; yet when mixed together, one knows their place.
The intent does not reside in words, yet the responsive mechanism arrives accordingly. Thus we know that in transmitting the Buddha’s mind-seal, there has never been any separate doctrine.
Ānanda, fearing further difficulties from others, asked: "Even though time and place may be relied upon as evidence, is it only you alone who have heard this, or [have others also heard it]?"
Many people heard it together, not just I alone: there were ten thousand bhikṣus, two thousand bodhisattvas,
eighty thousand elders, and six trillion devas, nāgas, and others, so as to avoid the difficulty of Duḥśīla hearing it by himself.
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by the fourfold assembly and preached for the great multitude a Mahāyāna sūtra titled *The Single Flavor,
Reality, Signlessness, Non-arising, Determination of the Ultimate Reality, Primordial Awakening, and Beneficial Practice*. If anyone hears this sūtra,
or even receives and upholds a single four-line verse from it, such a person shall enter the ground of the Buddha’s wisdom and be able to teach and transform sentient beings through skillful means.
Having been born, he acts as a great spiritual friend to all sentient beings.

Among the sūtras spoken by the Buddha, there are five distinct flavors, namely: the flavor of milk, the flavor of curd, the flavor of fresh butter, the flavor of clarified butter, and the flavor of *sarpis* (ghee).
This sūtra is purely of the flavor of *sarpis* and possesses no other flavor; that it has no other flavor means—
This is precisely the true mind; the Buddha and sentient beings are fundamentally identical, yet sentient beings are entirely deluded while the Buddhas are entirely awakened.

Since the sages abide between these two states of delusion and awakening, my original teacher directly used the Vajrasamādhi to completely shatter their delusions so that they might attain the ultimate state;
for this reason, he preached it. Because the true mind is signless, it is the source from which all phenomena arise.
Relying on the eye, it is called the True Nature of the Dharma-body, which is unborn yet unimpededly gives rise to all things; this is called the Dharma-nature of the Dharma-body.

It is signless, like empty space; as empty space is signless yet universally contains the myriad existents, so the Dharma-nature is unborn yet like heaven and earth—though heaven and earth are unborn, they do not hinder the arising of the myriad things. Thus, for the sake of sentient beings, the Buddha [manifests].
Because written characters express and manifest the affairs of beings, provisional names are established. If we accord with the ultimate meaning, that which is prior to words cannot be apprehended;
it is definitively nothing other than the single true aspect (*dharmatā*). Why is it that one does not speak of "signlessness" (*animitta*) but speaks of the "true aspect"?
It is because I fear that people might fail to understand the meaning of signlessness as emptiness, and thus fall into views of existence and non-existence; therefore, I speak [of the true aspect].

As for the true mark (*dharmatā*), why is it considered "real"? It is because the original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*) inherent in every person ultimately admits of nothing else—just as the eye cannot admit dust, or fire cannot admit water.

Why is it called "beneficial practice" (*artha-caryā*)? What is called original enlightenment and beneficial practice is precisely what the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* refers to as the "wondrous clarity of original enlightenment.
Regarding the previous statement that there is no form and no arising, if one were to grasp at this with fixed attachment...
If one were to claim that "formlessness" implies falling into the heterodox views of nihilism or eternalism, how could one know that the Dharma-body is formless yet nothing is not encompassed by it;
that the nature of phenomena is unborn yet nothing is not born from it; that the true mind is unconditioned yet nothing is not enacted by it;
and that Prajñā is non-cognizing yet nothing is unknown to it? Now, because fundamental enlightenment is wondrously luminous, it is thus.
This eye of beneficial conduct sees thus and hears thus; it has never been within the reach of mental deliberation or verbal discussion.
To briefly fix the mind upon it constitutes a delusive thought, for it is not the primordial awakening (*mūla-bodhi*).

Because it is wondrously luminous, it occurs spontaneously without being sought, occurring without knowing how it occurs. Zhuangzi’s characterization of "non-knowing" as "spontaneity" (*ziran*) seems slightly off the mark.
Once you have grasped this, although it is so, you must know that such a commentary is like adding legs to a snake. Why?
Long ago, when the World-Honored One ascended the seat in silence, Mañjuśrī struck the gavel and said: "Observe closely the Dharma of the Dharma-King; the Dharma of the Dharma-King is thus.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One descended from the seat. If this were the case, how could the World-Honored One have spoken of "one flavor"?

Ultimate reality, signlessness, non-arising, the definitive limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), primordial enlightenment (*ādikṣānti*), and beneficial conduct—all these together constitute this very commentary.
Were it not for Mañjuśrī’s discernment, students would often miss the mark.
If a person upholds this single phrase of the True Sutra before the World-Honored One has even opened his mouth, that person enters the stage of Buddha-wisdom.

Regarding those who realize the true mark for themselves: once they have realized the truth, they understand how to employ skillful means to act as great spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) to sentient beings.
Why is this? If there were only the real and no skillful means, the capacity to guide would not be extensive;

if there were only skillful means and no reality, it would ultimately be difficult to reach the final goal. Since both the real and the skillful are applied together to benefit those of the three capacities equally, how could they not be considered true spiritual friends?
After the Buddha had spoken this sutra, he sat in the full lotus posture and immediately entered the Vajra Samādhi, his body and mind unmoving.
In the preceding passage, he used words to reveal the principle that transcends words;

thus the ancients said, "He spoke of that which cannot be spoken," yet students ultimately remain stuck in verbal explanations. Now, however, by sitting cross-legged and entering meditative absorption, he [demonstrates] through non-...
These words reveal that which is beyond speech, directly causing the paths of thought to cease and the way of language to be cut off;
it is not reached by supernatural powers. Mañjuśrī could not emerge from the woman’s samādhi, nor can one arrive there through meditative absorption.
Even Samantabhadra with his Universal Eye cannot see the body of Samantabhadra, for it cannot be distinguished by words. Vimalakīrti remained silent at Vaiśālī, for this is neither world nor self.
"It may be inferred that the World-Honored One’s concealment of his traces in Magadha was none other than the Vajra-samādhi.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu in the assembly named Āgada who rose from his seat, joined his palms,
knelt with his right knee on the ground, and wishing to proclaim this meaning, spoke in verse:
In the preceding passage, when the World-Honored One entered samādhi after speaking the sutra, although there were words, they ultimately returned to wordlessness.
Here, the bhikṣu named Agada—the Sanskrit term for which has not yet been translated—is intended to convey a manifold meaning; it signifies "wordlessness.
Being wordless means there is no speaking; yet, while there is no speaking, it does not preclude the recitation of verses in response to the Buddha.

What is called "speaking" is itself non-speaking, and non-speaking is itself speaking; it is neither biased nor parched, neither leaking nor stagnant, but is the perfectly integrated Middle Way, sovereign in this way.
O Honored One whose Great Compassion is fulfilled, your wisdom penetrates all without obstruction, for the sake of extensively delivering all sentient beings.
I teach the meaning of the single truth, all by means of the flavor of the one path. Ultimately, I do not rely on the meanings and flavors spoken in the Hīnayāna;

all such things are entirely devoid of reality. I cause [beings] to enter the stage of the Buddhas' wisdom—the definitive true limit— so that all who hear it transcend the world, and there are none who do not attain liberation.

Loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is able to bestow happiness, and compassion (*karuṇā*) is able to extract suffering; these two are common to the three vehicles (*triyāna*). However, because those [of the three vehicles] harbor them within their hearts through attachment and views (*sneha-dṛṣṭi*), they are not called "fulfilled.
How could this compare to the World-Honored One’s unconditioned compassion (*nirālambana-karuṇā*), which does not discriminate between enemies and kin but delivers all equally?

Therefore, it is called "Great" and "Fulfilled. Regarding wisdom (*prajñā*), there are two types: first, the "Treasure" (*ratna*); second, the "Skillful Means" (*upāya*). These two are common to the three vehicles.

The Śrāvakas who enter the Dharma-nature cling to the real and are deluded regarding the provisional; thus they are said to be biased toward emptiness. The Bodhisattvas cling to the provisional and are hindered by the real; thus they are said to be "degrees of phenomena.
The World-Honored One first used the great [teaching] to match their capacity and subsequently guided them with the small;

he began by opening the provisional from within the real, and finally discarded the provisional to reveal the real. Throughout this process, there was the responding to the provisional and the provisional responding to the real, as well as the responding to the real and the real responding to the real.
Because he guides and transforms beings without fixed direction, he is called "unimpeded. The Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) delivers people like a sheep-cart carrying men;

the Middle Vehicle and the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna) may be understood as having limited transformations. How can these compare to the World-Honored One, who uses the unimpeded vehicle of empty space to deliver beings?
Therefore, he is said to "broadly deliver" those of the Three Vehicles, using the wisdom of partial realization to match his own understanding in order to save all sentient beings.
It is not that [the Buddha] does not wish to deliver beings extensively, but rather because his power is insufficient. The World-Honored One’s wisdom is unimpeded;

he teaches the One Vehicle as immeasurable vehicles, yet the ultimate is merely the Single Truth. This Single Truth is identical to the Single Mind. This mind is what Buddhas and sentient beings alike receive;
its flavor is authentic and true, like clarified butter (*sarpis*), and is not like the four preceding flavors where the Great and Small Vehicles are separated.
Therefore, one is able to extensively deliver [beings] through the explained flavor of meaning; "meaning" refers to the single truth (*ekasatya*), and its "flavor" is that of the *amṛta* (nectar).

The single truth has no second truth; it is a single flavor, not a mixed flavor. Being neither dual nor mixed, it is entirely free from unreality. Since it is free from unreality, to what destination should one go?
Because it is free from unreality, one goes to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and enters the Buddha-wisdom; this is indeed appropriate. As it is said:
This Dharma is rare and difficult to encounter; if one should encounter it—whether seeing or hearing it—one will all attain supramundane liberation.
The bhikṣu has already spoken two verses above to praise it before the assembly; hereafter, he exhorts the assembly to inquire extensively.
Immeasurable bodhisattvas all deliver sentient beings; for the sake of the multitude, they ask extensively and deeply about the Dharma’s mark of quiescence.
Entering the state of certainty, the Tathāgata’s wisdom and skillful means shall be explained as the entry into reality.
All are in accord with the Single Vehicle (Ekayāna); there are no diverse flavors.
Just as a single rain moistens all grasses so that they all flourish, so too the moisture of the Dharma of a single flavor,
according to their diverse natures, pervades and fills all beings. As that single rain moistens them all,
causing the sprouts of Bodhi to grow, they enter the diamond-like samādhi and realize the true concentration of the Dharma.
To decisively sever doubt and remorse, the seal of the One Dharma is established.
The preceding section has concluded the praise; from here below, the inquiry is exhorted. The selection states: "The wisdom of the Bodhisattvas is profound and their resolve is firm;

they have already accomplished their own deliverance with abundance. Why then must they ask further? The meaning is that while the Bodhisattvas take the salvation of sentient beings as their primary concern, if they do not inquire extensively, [the teachings will not be fully realized].
How could one with limited capacity and understanding possibly equal the vastness of the World-Honored One?

For this reason, in the following text, all the bodhisattvas—such as Vimuktiprabha and others—initiate their inquiries through exhortation. Because they ask extensively, they come to know the quiescence of all phenomena; because they know this quiescence, they enter the state of certainty.
This is the realization of true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*). Having realized true wisdom, they must then inquire regarding the Tathāgata’s provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*).

One who clearly understands provisional wisdom should be like the Tathāgata’s skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), wherein all provisional means are gathered to enter into reality and accord with the Single Vehicle (*ekayāna*) without any admixture of flavors.
To use a metaphor: it is like the rain from heaven, which is of a single flavor and equal for all;
yet, while the roots, stalks, and sizes of grasses and trees differ, they each receive benefit differently—not that the rain itself possesses such distinctions.
I, the Tathāgata, preach the Dharma with a single voice, yet sentient beings each understand it according to their own kind.
Although these various understandings differ, in the ultimate sense, they are all nothing other than the sprouting of the Bodhi of the One Vehicle.
To enter this Vajra Samādhi, sever doubt, and give rise to faith—there is no other seal than this.

Chapter Two: On the Dharma of Signlessness At that time, the World-Honored One arose from samādhi and spoke these words: "The ground of the wisdom of all Buddhas enters into the true nature of dharmas and their definitive reality;
therefore, skillful means and supernatural powers are all signless. This benefit of the single, awakened realization of the ultimate meaning is difficult to understand and difficult to enter."

This is not something known or seen by those of the two vehicles; only Buddhas and Bodhisattvas can know it. For all sentient beings who can be saved, [the Buddha] preaches a single flavor (*ekarasa*).

In the preceding chapter, the compilers of the collection first recorded that the World-Honored One’s preaching of the Dharma is of a single flavor, true, signless (*animitta*), and unborn (*anutpāda*).
Raising up [the staff] to show it to people, his intent lies before words; those of sharp faculties act upon seeing the shadow of the whip without waiting for further explanation.
Fearing that those of middling or inferior capacity might not believe or understand, the World-Honored One arose from samādhi and spoke of his own accord, acting as an uninvited friend.
That which enters into the characteristics of the true Dharma and its definitive nature is the self-nature of all Buddhas.
The realm of the stage of noble awakened wisdom is such that only Buddhas can exhaustively fathom it; it does not admit of understanding by others. This is what constitutes true wisdom. Why is this?

It is because this matter is a realm that cannot be reached through words or language; were it not for entering meditative absorption, how could one sever all doubts? This passage describes the act of emerging from concentration to demonstrate the state of having entered it.
Why so? Because this matter is not a domain accessible through written characters or speech; if one does not enter meditative absorption, how could one decisively cut through the multitude of doubts?
What is called "expedient means and supernormal powers" refers to provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*).
It points back to what was previously termed the single flavor of reality—truthful, signless, and unborn—which, within its own nature, is fundamentally ineffable.

Nevertheless, for the sake of sentient beings, one establishes provisional teachings based on the ultimate reality, employing unimpeded wisdom and spiritual penetration to explain various names and characteristics through expedient means.

These names and meanings, though provisional and not ultimate, cannot lead one to the ultimate without being provisional; yet the provisional does not exist as provisional in itself, but exists for the purpose of manifesting the ultimate.
Likewise, the ultimate does not exist as ultimate in itself, but exists for the purpose of dispelling the provisional.
Both of these flow from the stage of the Buddhas’ self-awakening; they are both signless, a single awakening, and the definitive meaning. By means of the three... [text ends]
Because the vehicles and views are separated and the provisional and the real are difficult to harmonize, it is said that this is difficult to understand and difficult to enter.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Liberation rose from his seat, joined his palms, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"O Honored One, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, when the True Dharma has departed from the world and the Semblance Dharma remains during the final kalpa, among the sentient beings of the five turbidities..."
With many evil karmas, we cycle through the three realms with no time of escape;
we pray that the Buddha, out of compassion, will proclaim for future sentient beings the single flavor of definitive truth, so that those beings may equally attain liberation.
This Bodhisattva is named "Liberated One" because, through the Buddha’s entry into meditative absorption, he profoundly realized the truth;
thus, all his various doubts and delusions ceased to be a burden, and for this reason he is called "Liberated. There are two reasons for his inquiry:
first, because he was exhorted by the bhikṣu Agada to ask extensive and profound questions; second, because having himself attained liberation, he felt compassion [for others].

Furthermore, I ask this for the sake of those who have yet to attain liberation in the future. While the Buddha was in the world, he taught and transformed beings himself without waiting for my questions;
however, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, when the True Dharma has passed and the Semblance Dharma prevails, those sentient beings will not be able to receive his sublime instructions in person.
Upon what shall they rely? In the age of the Final Dharma, sentient beings will be without rescue and without refuge.

Relying on those who are without refuge, and further compounded by the five turbidities, the density of strife, and the stubbornness of contention, there will be no teacher or Dharma upon which to rely;

thus, people will mistakenly create evil karma and wander through saṃsāra without return. Therefore, we entreat the World-Honored One to preemptively suspend the mirror of the Dharma to illuminate the future, so that beings may recognize the right path and attain equal liberation.

The Buddha said, "Good son, that you are able to ask me about the cause for transcending the world, desiring to transform sentient beings so that they may attain the fruit of transcending the world—this is a great matter, inconceivable, due to great kindness and great compassion.
If I were not to speak, I would fall into stinginess and greed. Listen with a single mind; I shall proclaim it for you."

Regarding the explanation of the cause for transcending the world, the *Lotus Sūtra* states: "The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world for the sake of one great causal matter (*eka-kāraṇa-artha*).
What is called this 'one great matter' is precisely the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddha-jñāna-darśana*). Sentient beings are deluded regarding the Buddha’s...
Because of their knowledge and vision, they enter into birth and death; because the Buddhas have entered the Buddha-knowledge and vision, they realize nirvana.

Because they have realized nirvana, they abide in immeasurable bliss; because they enter into birth and death, they undergo immeasurable suffering. Therefore, the World-Honored One praised you, saying:
"If you did not possess great compassion, how could you be able to inquire about this inconceivable matter? Since you, through your compassion..."
Out of compassion for the sake of the multitudes, I shall now, with a mind of great joy and equanimity, explain this to you.
Noble son, if one transforms sentient beings without giving rise to the notion of transformation, and without the non-arising of non-transformation, that transformation is truly great.

It causes those sentient beings to all be free from the "self" of the mind; for the "self" of all minds is fundamentally empty and quiescent. If one attains the emptiness of the mind, then the mind [is liberated].
When there is no illusion, no magical creation, and no transformation, one immediately attains the mind of non-arising; this mind of non-arising abides in non-transformation.
Since the World-Honored One has granted permission to speak of this, fearing that others might fail to understand and fall into the duality of subject and object, he says:

"If one transforms sentient beings, there is no arising within that transformation. If one harbors a mind that acts as the transformer, then the beings being transformed will involve themselves in attachment and false views.
Because such transformation would be limited and thus not commensurate with great compassion, the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:

"All classes of sentient beings whatsoever, I shall cause to enter *nirvāṇa* without remainder and bring them to liberation. Although in this way I liberate immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings, in reality there is no sentient being who has been liberated.
Why is this? It continues: "Why is this... [The text here implies the subsequent reasoning regarding the non-existence of a self and the nature of emptiness.]
If a bodhisattva perceives the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, or the mark of a life-span, they are not a bodhisattva;

yet, they do not give rise to a non-conceptualized state. Why? Because if one gives rise to a non-conceptualized state, one does not connect with the realm of sentient beings, and compassion has nothing to bestow.
As the Book of Documents says: "What does Heaven speak? The four seasons proceed. What does Heaven speak?
Ah! All things are nurtured therein; truly, it is through desirelessness and silence that one perceives the great transformation of Heaven and Earth.

If Heaven were to say, "I am able to nurture all things," or if Earth were to say, "I am able to support all things," their capacity would be narrow and small—how could they be called possessed of great virtue?
Although they speak not, the people of the world attribute the source of their achievement to them, and thus all credit is returned to Heaven.
Because of this ground, only the Buddhas—having transcended both the transformer and the transformed—encompass the great trichiliocosm with their merit, which rivals that of heaven and earth.
Since there is neither a transformer nor a transformed, how can they be said to "transform sentient beings"? In truth, there is nothing to be transformed;
the Sages understand that all the bodies and minds of sentient beings are neither body nor mind, yet through the deluded attachments of ignorance, beings undergo birth in vain.
The skillful means for death are revealed to cause one to abandon the "mine" of the mind. Regarding the "mind-self," the self is precisely the physical body, and the body is a conditioned reflection.

As stated in the *Perfect Enlightenment Sutra*: "To falsely identify the four elements as the characteristic of one's own body, and the reflections of the six sense-objects as the characteristic of one's own mind.
How are these revealed? The body is like a phantom or a bubble; it takes form only upon meeting with conditions.
When conditions are exhausted, the mind ceases—like sparks from a stone, it does not abide for even a moment.

To realize in a single thought that its very substance is empty and quiescent is what is called the "false body and mind. If one attains the empty mind, this is what is called the "ever-abiding true mind.
It is not like the four elements or the reflected images of conditions, which are illusory and unreal; because it is eternally real, it is without illusion and without [ceasing].

Having transformed this which is neither illusory nor subject to transformation, one immediately attains the mind of non-arising; the nature of this non-arising mind is inherently quiescent, and it cannot be transformed by another.
The Bodhisattva Liberation then addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, the nature of the minds of sentient beings is fundamentally empty and quiescent. It is empty and quiescent.
“The essence of the mind has no form or characteristics; how may one cultivate it to attain the original empty mind? I pray that the Buddha, out of compassion, will explain this for me.

Upon hearing these words, the Bodhisattva said: “If one attains the empty mind such that the mind does not undergo illusory transformation, then one will know that the nature of the minds of sentient beings is fundamentally [empty].”
"Coming is empty and still; where there is emptiness and stillness, no marks of form can be sought. When there is nothing to seek, how can one cultivate and attain the original empty mind?
The Buddha said: "The Bodhisattva’s all mental marks are originally without basis. This original non-basis is itself empty and still, and without arising."
If the mind is without arising, one immediately enters emptiness and stillness; with a ground of mind that is empty and still, one attains the emptiness of mind.
Good son, the signless mind is without mind and without self, and all phenomena are likewise so.
The Buddha replied: "What was said regarding the nature of the mind being fundamentally empty is a provisional expression made for the sake of liberating sentient beings.
The ultimate, true meaning is that it is originally without a basis; because there is no basis, there is no location, and thus it is empty and quiescent.

Because there is no basis, there is no arising, and because there is no location, one directly realizes one's own mind. To have no location and no basis is to enter into emptiness and quiescence—this is what is meant by 'the mind wishing to take an object.'"

When thought is forgotten, the mouth desires to speak yet words fail; because there is no mutual correspondence, it cannot be known through cognition, and because there is no mind, it cannot be known through wisdom.

To thoroughly comprehend the characteristics of the mind is to realize that in both extremes there is no self to be found—what the ancients called "when a single thought does not arise, the whole body is fully manifested.
The Bodhisattva previously relied on the three vehicles for cultivation and refinement, clinging to existence.
Those who have attained realization through the cultivation of body and mind may now hear the sudden teaching of the One Vehicle that body and mind are fundamentally empty and quiescent;
yet, because their understanding of non-cultivation and non-attainment is not yet decisive, they raise this question. The World-Honored One’s intention is this:

my statement that [body and mind] are "fundamental" or "not fundamental" is still an expression of affirmative designation (*paryāya*). If one realizes that these are merely names without substantial reality, then...
"Since the mind has already been realized as empty, why need one further speak of cultivation or non-cultivation, realization or non-realization?

The Bodhisattva Vimukta addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, if there are any among all sentient beings who possess a self or who possess a mind, by what dharma should they be awakened so that those beings may escape from these bonds?"

Continuing from the previous response, regarding the Bodhisattva’s understanding that the nature of the mind is empty and quiescent, fundamentally devoid of cultivation or realization, yet possessing the principle and fruit [of enlightenment]—if this were so in theory, how could it be otherwise in practice?

Why is this? If all sentient beings currently cling to the existence of body and mind, we do not know what Dharma the World-Honored One would teach them to bring about awakening and enable their liberation from these bonds.
The Buddha said: "Good son, if there is one who holds to a self, cause them to contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination.

Since the twelve links of dependent origination fundamentally arise from cause and effect, and that which is produced by cause and effect arises from mental formations, if even the mind does not exist, how much less could the body exist?
If there is one who holds to a self, cause them to extinguish the view of existence; if there is one who holds to no-self, cause them to extinguish the view of non-existence. If the mind arises..."

If the nature of cessation and arising were such that when the mind ceases it causes the nature of cessation to cease, then this seeing-nature would immediately enter the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

Why is this? That which is originally produced does not cease; that which is originally ceased is not produced. What is neither produced nor ceased, and neither arises nor perishes—such is the characteristic of all dharmas. It is likewise so.

The twelve links of dependent origination take their initial commencement as the primary cause (*hetu*) and their auxiliary conditions as the contributing conditions (*pratyaya*). They mysteriously pervade the three periods of time.

Due to delusion, one turns one's back on one’s own mind; this is called ignorance (*avidyā*). The lack of awareness within ignorance is called volitional formations (*saṃskāra*). These two links belong to the past causes.

That which moves while remaining unmoving, giving rise to false discrimination, is called consciousness (*vijñāna*). That which conditions without there being an object of condition is called name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), consisting of the sense faculties and their objects.

The meeting [of conditions] is called the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). The mutual encounter of the faculties and their objects is called contact (*sparśa*). The experiencing of suffering or pleasure is called feeling (*vedanā*). These five factors belong to the present fruit.
From feeling, the arising of aversion and attachment is called craving (*tṛṣṇā*). Because of aversion and attachment, the performance of future karma is called grasping (*upādāna*).
The accumulation of karma within the three realms is called existence (*bhava*). These three factors belong to the present cause. [They result in] the feelings of the three realms.
Birth is called birth; birth, old age, and death follow one another. These two links belong to the future fruit, taking karma as the cause and the reception of retribution as the fruit.
Such causes and effects all arise from the non-awakening of ignorance, whereby the deluded mind grasps and rejects.

Now, observing the phenomena born of conditions, they do not abide through the three periods of time and do not remain for even a single kṣaṇa. Where, then, is there a mind? Since the mind does not exist...

There are those who, due to the mind’s false fabrications, construct an illusory body; one should contemplate its extinction. Thus, the *Awakening of Mahāyāna* (*Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*) states:

"Since the four great elements have each returned to their respective origins, where now does this illusory body reside? By means of these twelve links of dependent origination, one should investigate back and forth:
which among them is the self? If sentient beings cling to the notion of a self, that [clinging] is ignorance (*avidyā*). It is the self.

If one asks whether the sequence from consciousness and name-and-form up to birth, old age, sickness, death, and so forth is the self—if each individual element were the self, there would be twelve selves;
if each individual element were not the self, then [the view] that the collection is the self is refuted for those ordinary persons who cling to a self.
As for those of the Two Vehicles and non-Buddhists who cling to "no-self," they [are refuted by the fact that] these are produced by causes and conditions.

The nature of birth should be separate from the mind; if it were separate from the mind, then the absence of self would be identical to external objects, and as such, it would not be my concern—who could then determine its existence or non-existence?
If the absence of self were identical with the mind, then it would perish along with the causes and conditions [of the mind].

If it perished along with them, then all that is manifested would be utterly non-existent. If all were utterly non-existent, then who is it that knows there is no self? And who is it that knows there is no one to know?
Without cause, they allow for the extinction of the view of non-existence; yet others again hold the attachment that causes and conditions of the past and future all arise from the mind.

Having already known that they arise from the mind, one should further know that the mind itself is fundamentally without arising. Because it exists prior to objects, if there were no objects, its arising would likewise be unobtainable.
If the followers of the Two Vehicles cling to the mind as being eternally extinguished and non-arising, they fail to realize that the mind is fundamentally perfect and pervasive.
Non-arising does not arise; it is through false attachment that error is formed. If one knows this error, false attachment is naturally dispelled. Therefore, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says:
"Mahāmati, I speak of the cessation of the characteristics of the ālayavijñāna, not the cessation of its nature.
If its nature were to cease, the beginningless flow would be severed; yet this nature of the ālaya does not truly cease. To say it ceases is to see its nature; it is not what I mean by 'clarity'."
The view that perceives the nature through the mind is precisely the attachment to existence, non-existence, arising, and ceasing.

If this view is extinguished, one enters the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). Why? Because the original birth does not cease; since the true permanence of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) is beyond cessation, there is nothing to be ceased.

That which is originally extinguished does not arise; it does not abide for even a single moment (*kṣaṇa*), and since there is no arising, there is nothing to arise. For this reason, my mind externally extends to the myriad phenomena.
"Because all phenomena and so forth are equally non-arising, it is said that they are likewise thus.
The Bodhisattva Vimukta addressed the Buddha, saying: "Venerable One, if there are sentient beings who see phenomena arising, what kind of view causes them to cease?
And if they see phenomena ceasing, what kind of view causes them to cease?"

For those who previously held the view of a self, have them contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination; since these links are without arising, they arise only through the delusions of the mind.
If the mind undergoes birth and cessation, one must extinguish that deluded mind. If phenomena undergo birth and cessation, what view is there to be extinguished?
The Buddha said: "If there are sentient beings who, upon seeing dharmas arise, cause the view of non-existence to cease;

and when they see dharmas perish, cause the view of existence to cease; and by ceasing these views, they attain the true source of dharmas, which is the definitive nature of non-entrance and the certainty of non-arising."
Regarding phenomena, phenomena are without the cause of arising; it is through the mind that views are formed.

If those ordinary beings grasp at phenomena as fundamentally non-existent, yet see phenomena arising moment by moment—how could they be eternally non-existent? This causes them to extinguish the view of non-existence.

If those ordinary beings grasp at phenomena as fundamentally existent, yet see phenomena perishing and decaying moment by moment—how could they be eternally existent? This causes them to extinguish the view of existence. As for whether phenomena exist or do not exist...

Through meditative concentration, one knows that phenomena lack intrinsic nature; because they lack intrinsic nature, they are unarisen; and because they are unarisen, there is no seeing. Why is this so?
It is like the mutual exclusion of light and darkness: when it is night there is no light, and when it is day there is no darkness.

Worldly people do not understand this and each gives rise to fixed attachments. The wise person points out to them: "You say there is no light; yet when light arises, the characteristic of light manifests before you."
How can you say that when [light] is absent, it is simply non-existent? You claim there is light; yet when this light is about to perish, the characteristic of darkness manifests before you.
Where, then, is the light that was about to perish? Light and darkness mutually displace one another; what concern has empty space with them?

The presence or absence of these sensory objects is their own internal affair—what concern does it have for the mind? Since the mind is not concerned with them, when they arise and perish, you should realize [their emptiness].

The dharmas are fundamentally empty; one should know that the mind’s false conceptualization has ceased and its false perceptions have vanished. Nevertheless, one must not dogmatically cling to existence or non-existence.
If a dharma were definitively existent, it should never become non-existent—how could it then abide for even a single moment?
If a dharma were definitively non-existent, it should never become existent—how could it then arise from moment to moment? Therefore, it is said that there is no entry into a fixed nature.
The Bodhisattva Vimukta addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, you cause those sentient beings to abide in non-arising;
is this non-arising itself? The Buddha said: "Abiding in non-arising is precisely arising. Why is this? Non-abiding and non-arising are what constitute true non-arising.
If a bodhisattva gives rise to non-arising, then by the arising of that arising, both arising and ceasing are extinguished together; thus, original birth does not exist."
The mind that arises is eternally empty and quiescent; being empty and quiescent, it has no dwelling place. That the mind has no dwelling is precisely non-arising (*anutpāda*).
If one says that dwelling in non-arising is itself non-arising, then there would be a non-arising in which one could dwell.

If there is a non-arising to dwell in, that is a "dharma" (an existent thing). If there is a dharma, there is dwelling; if there is dwelling, there is arising, not non-arising. Non-dwelling and non-arising—this is indeed non-arising.

The words that dispel both [arising and ceasing] are as follows: If one holds that the mind capable of arising in the preceding moment extinguishes the dharma produced in the succeeding moment, this is precisely "arising.
If one holds that the thought capable of extinguishing in the succeeding moment extinguishes the dharma already extinguished in the preceding moment, this is precisely "ceasing.
If it were thus, they would merely be called "arising and ceasing"; how could they be "non-arising"? One must simply cause arising...
When both cessation and the ceasing mind are eternally empty and quiescent, one neither dwells in arising nor dwells in cessation;
when the two extremes are severed, the middle is naturally void.
The Bodhisattva Liberation then addressed the Buddha, saying: "Venerable One, since the mind has no dwelling place, what is there to cultivate or learn? To this, the Buddha replied: "There is."
"Is this training or is it beyond training? The Buddha said, "The bodhisattva’s mind of non-arising has no coming or going;
it is fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha, quiescent and unmoving. It is neither in training nor beyond training. There is no training and no non-training;
this is 'beyond training' (aśaikṣa). Yet it is not that there is no training; this is what constitutes 'that which is trained'."
If the mind has no dwelling place, it is transcendent and self-attained, not achieved through study;

yet the World-Honored One has often exhorted people to practice and learn—is this for those who are still learning (*śaikṣa*) or for those beyond learning (*aśaikṣa*)? The intent of the World-Honored One was this:
"I exhort people to practice and learn because of the mind of non-arising, which is neither internal nor external, being fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha, which people cannot realize on their own."

Because they know that the views of internal and external existence and non-existence arise from inverted攀緣 (ālambana/objects of perception), I urge them to realize and witness their own minds and enter the ground of the unborn.
This is because they are not yet learners (śaikṣa), as they have not yet abandoned external longings; nor are they non-learners (aśaikṣa), as they must personally and closely observe their own minds.
If one has been deluded and turned away from one's own mind for a long time, how can one succeed unless one approaches it repeatedly?

Because one realizes the non-arising [of phenomena], there is no distinct training; this is precisely what constitutes "no-more-learning" (*aśaikṣa*), for it is by training in that which is not to be trained that one attains it.
It does not mean that the absence of anything to be trained is itself the training.
The Bodhisattva Vimukta addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, why is the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha quiescent and immovable? The Buddha said:

"The Tathāgatagarbha is the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha that is quiescent and immovable because the characteristics of arising, ceasing, deliberation, and cognition obscure the principle, so that it is not manifest."
The Tathāgatagarbha has two aspects: first, that which resides within the bonds of sentient beings, obscured by birth and death; second, that which has emerged from the bonds.
Furthermore, there are three types: the empty Tathāgatagarbha, the non-empty Tathāgatagarbha, and the empty-and-non-empty Tathāgatagarbha.
Because the Buddhas have perfectly realized and clearly manifested these without obstruction, they are able to enter birth and death to provide salvation and protection.
Sentient beings, shrouded by ignorance, die here and are born there; they do not even know this for themselves, so how could they transform others?
Although they lack such knowledge, their fundamental nature has never wavered. Because it is unwavering, one is exhorted to repeatedly draw near to and study this immovability.
It neither emerges nor enters; this is that which is to be studied, a study without distinction.

The Bodhisattva Dhimukti addressed the Buddha, saying, "Venerable One, how is it that the characteristics of discursive thought and cognition arise and perish? The Buddha said, "For a Bodhisattva, there is no such thing as 'not having' [discursive thought].
If one were to have such a state of 'having or not having,' then the arising of various thoughts—thousands of reflections and myriad deliberations—is itself the arising and perishing."

When a Bodhisattva contemplates the characteristic of the original nature, the principle is inherently complete; to engage in a thousand thoughts and ten thousand deliberations does not benefit the Way, but merely causes agitation and confusion, losing the sovereign of the fundamental mind.
When the faculties and objects are in suchness, the nature of mind is non-cognizant; consciousness follows conditions to deliberate, giving rise to false discrimination based on those conditions.
When manifesting, it arises; when conditions disperse, it ceases. Both arising and ceasing depend upon the self; how could there be any false recognition?

If one takes the true principle of one's own mind to be hidden, then as one follows along with conditioned thoughts, arising and ceasing are clearly evident. Yet if one follows along with the true principle, they cannot be found at all.
Sentient beings, by taking the delusive to be themselves, give rise to various thoughts, even to thousands of reflections and ten thousand deliberations.
Since deliberation is always characterized by arising and ceasing, our World-Honored One exhorts all Bodhisattvas that they must constantly contemplate principle.
When one contemplates principle, principle itself becomes self-sufficient; the mind-king dwells in its own sovereign hall, lofty and autonomous.

One should not follow after phenomena, for to follow phenomena is to engage in a thousand thoughts and ten thousand deliberations that do not benefit the Way, causing the mind-king to be turned by external objects and lose its mastery.
Regarding "receiving the instructions of others," the *Śūraṃgama-sūtra* states: "The self-mind grasps the self-mind; it is not that non-illusion becomes illusory phenomena.
All these sayings refer to the fact that the mind follows after objects.
If there is no discursive thought, then there is no arising or ceasing; as reality is, the various consciousnesses do not arise, and the flow of the stream is tranquil and non-arising.
Attaining the purity of these five dharmas is called the Mahāyāna Bodhisattva’s entry into the purity of the five dharmas. When the mind is pure, there is no delusion;
when there is no delusion, one enters the stage of the Tathāgata’s self-realized noble wisdom. Entering this stage of wisdom means skillfully knowing that all things are fundamentally unborn;
knowing they are fundamentally unborn, one is free from false conceptualization.
Sentient beings follow after phenomena, whereby they give rise to discursive thoughts within and bring about arising and ceasing without.

When a Bodhisattva contemplates principle, discursive thoughts are extinguished within and arising and ceasing are forgotten without. When, in accordance with reality, neither the internal nor the external arise, then all consciousnesses are tranquil and still, and their continuous flow does not occur.
Consciousness is precisely discursive thought; the continuous flow is precisely arising and ceasing. This is "thought."
"Consciousness (manas) deliberates; discernment (vijñāna) cognizes; these are the eight consciousnesses. Birth-and-death (saṃskṛta) belongs to the five [sensory] consciousnesses.
Because this consciousness shares with the eight consciousnesses the inclusion of all mundane and supramundane seeds of birth-and-death, how could birth-and-death arise internally or externally?
Since there is no such state, one attains the purity of the five dharmas, as stated in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*: 'Do not grasp; there is nothing that is not illusion.'"
Even that which is not illusion does not arise; how then could illusory phenomena be established? Their meanings are identical to the five dharmas:

name, appearance, conceptualization, correct knowledge, and suchness. Sentient beings are the appearance of illusion; the Buddhas are called suchness. Sentient beings are called conceptualization; the Buddhas are called correct knowledge.
Correct knowledge remedies conceptualization, and suchness remedies the appearance of illusion; these two constitute the distinction.
Apart from this, there are ordinary beings and sages, superior and inferior; yet when combined, they are equal within the single designation of "illusion" and possess no substantial reality.

If one realizes that these are merely names and that there is no consciousness, then one realizes that the mind is fundamentally without delusion and enters the stage of the Tathāgata’s self-realized noble wisdom.
The Bodhisattva Vimukta addressed the Buddha, saying, "Venerable One, for one who is free from deluded thoughts, there should be no cessation.
The Buddha said, "For a Bodhisattva, delusion is fundamentally non-arising; there is no delusion to be ceased. Knowing that the mind is no-mind, there is no mind to be stilled.
Without division or distinction, the manifesting consciousness does not arise; since there is no arising, there is nothing to be ceased. This is neither cessation nor non-cessation. Why is this so?"
Therefore, cessation is itself non-cessation.

Having realized that the dharmas mentioned above are without arising or ceasing, the deluded mind engages in grasping and rejecting; yet one should know that the root of delusion is originally empty, and thus there should be no cessation.
The Buddha said: "You say that because there are no deluded thoughts, there is no cessation; but how do you know that the root of delusion is originally unarisen? The mind, too, is likewise."
This absence of non-existence means that within, thoughts and deliberations do not arise; this absence of delusion means that without, one does not cling to arising and ceasing.

When thoughts and deliberations do not arise, there is no discrimination; when one does not cling to arising and ceasing, the manifesting consciousness does not arise. Since both internal and external are thus as they are, there is neither arising nor ceasing.
Thought can be stilled, yet there is nothing to be stilled—this is the "stopping" of non-stopping. It is not... [non-attainment].
If cessation is manifested by means of existence, then it is not a cessation of non-existence. Why?
Because cessation itself is without cessation.
The Bodhisattva Vimukta addressed the Buddha, saying: "Venerable One, if cessation is without cessation, then cessation is itself arising. What, then, is meant [by this]?"

The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Anutpāda: "A bodhisattva should bring this arising to rest. Once it has been brought to rest, there is no longer any resting, nor does one dwell in non-resting, nor does one dwell in non-dwelling. What, then, is this arising?"

"If the subsequent thought ceases the arising and ceasing of the preceding thought, then although that which is ceased—the arising and ceasing—has been stilled, the thought capable of ceasing it has already arisen;
how then can there be non-arising? The Buddha replied: "When the subsequent thought ceases the arising and ceasing of the preceding thought, it is indeed as you have asked:
the preceding ceasing and the subsequent arising are thus. However, once the arising and ceasing of the preceding thought have already ceased, then the subsequent thought [is capable of...]"
The mind that practices cessation does not abide anywhere because it arises and ceases; therefore, one speaks of cessation.

Since there is no arising or ceasing to be extinguished, there is likewise nothing that can cease nor anything upon which to cease.
