The Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta asked, "What are the six practices and vows? Please explain them. The Buddha said, "First is the practice of the ten stages of faith;
second is the practice of the ten abodes; third is the practice of the ten deeds; fourth is the practice of the ten dedications; fifth is the practice of the ten stages;
and sixth is the practice of equal enlightenment. Only those who practice in this manner can understand them."
Regarding the Ten Faiths, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "From the truly wondrous and perfect, one again gives rise to the truly wondrous and subtle faith that abides eternally.
All delusive thoughts are extinguished without remainder, and the Middle Way is purely true; this is called the Abiding in the Mind of Faith (*śraddhā-citta-vihāra*).

With true faith, one clearly understands that all are universally penetrating, and the three—aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*)—cannot act as obstructions. In this way, it extends even to the past and the future..."
Throughout countless kalpas of past lives, all habitual tendencies from the shedding and taking up of bodies manifest before him;
this son of good family is able to recollect them all without omission, which is called the Abiding of the Mind in Mindfulness.

This wondrous, perfect, and pure essence gives rise to true refinement, whereby beginningless habitual tendencies are integrated into a single, unified clarity; through this very clarity, he advances toward true purity.
The state of the mind of vigor is called the "Abiding Mind of Wisdom," which manifests before one as pure wisdom.

The state of the mind of wisdom is called the "Abiding Mind of Samādhi," which maintains the clarity of knowledge, pervading all with stillness and depth, and remaining eternally concentrated in wondrous tranquility. From this abiding in samādhi, the light of illumination arises;

its luminous nature penetrates deeply, such that there is only progress and no regression—this is called the "Non-regressing Mind. As the mind advances with ease, it maintains itself securely without loss. (10)
When the breath-energy of the Tathāgata intersects with one's own, it is called the "mind that protects the Dharma.

Through the clarity of awakening, one maintains this state and is able to use wondrous power to turn the Buddha’s compassionate light back toward the Buddha and abide therein. It is like two mirrors facing each other, wherein their wondrous reflections enter into one another in infinite layers;
this is called the "mind of dedication. As the mind-light secretly turns back, one attains the Buddha’s eternally concentrated, unsurpassed state.
Subtle purity and dwelling in the unconditioned, attaining non-forgetfulness, is called the "dwelling of the mind in precepts" (*śīla-citta-vihāra*).

Dwelling in mastery over the precepts, being able to roam throughout the ten directions and proceeding according to one's vows, is called the "dwelling of the mind in vows" (*praṇidhāna-citta-vihāra*).

Ānanda, this son of good family, by means of true skillful means, gives rise to these ten minds; their essence is refined and radiant, and their ten functions interpenetrate to perfectly accomplish a single mind—this is called [the *ekacittavihāra*].
In the stage of "Abiding in the Arising of the Mind," one illuminates the mind so that it is like pure lapis lazuli within which refined gold appears;

because one treads upon the former wondrous mind to form the ground, it is called the "Stage of Cultivating the Ground. In the "Stage of the Mind-Ground," both engagement and knowledge are fully clarified;

because one travels through the ten directions without obstruction, it is called the "Stage of Cultivating Practice. In the "Stage of Abiding in Practice," one shares the same reception of the Buddha’s vital energy as the Buddha himself, like the middle [of the body].
The physical body (skandha-kāya) seeks out its parents; through the subtle communion of faith, it enters the lineage of the Tathāgata, which is called the Dwelling of Noble Birth.

Having entered the womb of the Way, it personally serves the progeny of the Awakened One; when the human features are fully formed within the womb, it is called the Dwelling of Fulfillment of Expedient Means.

When its physical appearance resembles that of a Buddha and its mental characteristics are likewise identical, it is called the Dwelling of the Right Mind. On this day, body and mind are perfectly integrated.

The further increase [of these qualities] is called the Stage of Non-retrogression (*avinivartanīya-vihāra*). The simultaneous perfection of the ten marks of spiritual excellence is called the Stage of Youthful Truth (*kumārabhūta-vihāra*).
The formation of the body and emergence from the womb, becoming a true son of the Buddha, is called the Stage of the Dharma Prince (*dharmarāja-putra-vihāra*).

This signifies the attainment of full maturity, just as a great king of a nation delegates all state affairs to his crown prince; when that Kṣatriya prince has reached adulthood, he is entrusted with the governance.
Listing the names of the consecrations: the consecration of abiding in the stage of Ānanda;

having become a son of the Buddha, this good man is endowed with the immeasurable, sublime virtues of the Tathāgatas and accords with the ten directions, thus his conduct is named "Joyful"; he is well able to benefit all sentient beings, thus his conduct is named "Beneficial";
through self-awakening and awakening others, he attains freedom from opposition and resistance, thus his conduct is named "Free from Anger."

The practice of generating all types of conduct that extends to the limits of the future, which is equal throughout the three periods of time and pervasive throughout the ten directions, is called the "Inexhaustible Practice.
The attainment of various dharma-gates through universal harmony, without error or confusion, is called the "Practice Free from Delusion and Confusion.
Thus, within the state of sameness, one manifests a multitude of differences; yet each distinct characteristic is seen as being identical—this is called "Excellent Manifestation."
Practicing in this manner, extending even to the ten directions, one fills the empty space with atoms; within each and every atom, the worlds of the ten directions appear.
The appearance of the atoms and the appearance of the worlds do not obstruct or hinder one another—this is called the Practice of Non-Attachment.
Various manifestations appear before one, all of which are the foremost *pāramitā*—this is called the Practice of Reverence. Such perfect interfusion is able to accomplish the ten directions.

The rules and regulations of all Buddhas are called the Practice of Good Dharmas; each and every one is pure and without outflows, being the single true unconditioned nature that is inherently so, and is therefore called the Practice of Reality.

Ānanda, when this good man has perfected his supernatural powers and completed the task of becoming a Buddha, he will be pure, refined, and true, far removed from all lingering afflictions. He shall then deliver sentient beings and bring an end to all further crossings.

The dedication of turning back from conditioned phenomena with a mind directed toward the path of Nirvana is called the Dedication of Protecting and Delivering All Sentient Beings while Remaining Free from the Concept of Sentient Beings.
The dedication that destroys what can be destroyed and remains far removed from all notions of "separation" is called the Indestructible Dedication.

When fundamental awakening is serene and its realization is equal to the awakening of the Buddhas, it is called the Dedication Equal to All Buddhas. When the essence of reality is clarified and perfected, such that one’s ground is like that of a Buddha, it is called the Ground of the Buddha.

The dedication of the ground named "Reaching All Places" is the dedication of mutual penetration of worlds by Tathāgatas so as to attain non-obstruction, called the "Dedication of the Treasury of Inexhaustible Merit.
Within the stages that are identical to the Buddha-ground, each gives rise to causes of purity;
by manifesting these causes, one takes up the path to nirvāṇa, which is called the "Dedication of Roots of Goodness in Accordance with Equality."

Once the true roots are established, the sentient beings of the ten directions are all my own fundamental nature. This nature being perfectly fulfilled does not lose its designation as "sentient beings.
To accord with and contemplate all sentient beings equally, and to dedicate [merit] such that one is free from all marks—this alone, both in its engagement and its detachment, is nameless.
This is called the dedication to the mark of True Suchness (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa-pariṇāmanā*); it is truly attaining that which is as-it-is.

The unimpeded nature throughout the ten directions is called the dedication of liberation from bondage; the perfection of inherent virtues and the cessation of the measure of the dharma-realm is called the dedication of the immeasurable dharma-realm.

Ānanda, these sons of good have exhausted these forty-one pure minds and subsequently accomplish the four kinds of wondrously perfect preparatory practices (*prayoga*). They take the Buddha’s awakening as their own mind. If...
The "Emerging" and "Not Yet Emerging" stages are like drilling wood to produce fire; when one wishes to ignite the wood, it is called the Stage of Warmth (*uṣmagata*).

Furthermore, when one’s own mind attains Buddhahood, whether relying or not relying upon what has been traversed—like ascending a high mountain or entering the void with a slight obstruction remaining below—it is called the Stage of the Summit (*mūrdhan*).
When the mind and the Buddha are identical, one skillfully attains the Middle Way, like a person enduring hardship who harbors no resentment.

When names no longer arise, it is called the Stage of Patience (*kṣānti-bhūmi*). When the quantity [of conceptualization] is extinguished, the delusion within awakening and the Middle Way are both beyond designation;

this is called the Stage of the Supreme Worldly Dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma-bhūmi*). Ānanda, when this good man thoroughly attains penetration into Great Bodhi, and his awakening penetrates the Tathāgata’s exhaustive Buddha-realm, it is called the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
When distinct natures enter into sameness, and that very sameness is also extinguished—[this is the subsequent stage].

The stage named "Stainless" (*vimalā-bhūmi*) is the arising of extreme purity and brilliance; the stage named "Luminous" (*prabhākari-bhūmi*) is the fulfillment of extreme awakening through brilliance;

the stage named "Blazing Wisdom" (*arciṣmatī-bhūmi*) is that which cannot be reached by any similarities or differences; the stage named "Difficult to Conquer" (*sudurjayā-bhūmi*) is the nature-purity of unconditioned *tathatā* revealed in its clarity;
the stage named "Manifest" (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*) is the reaching of the limit of *tathatā*; the stage named "Far-Reaching" (*dūraṅgamā-bhūmi*) is the single mind of *tathatā*.
The manifestation of the function of True Suchness (*tathatā*) from the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*) is called the Good Wisdom Ground (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*).
Ānanda, from this point onward, these Bodhisattvas complete their cultivation and their merit becomes perfected; this ground is also termed the Stage of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-avasthā*).

The wondrous cloud of compassionate shade covers the ocean of *nirvāṇa*, and it is thus named the Dharma Cloud Ground (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*). While the Tathāgata flows against the current, such Bodhisattvas [flow with it].

Proceeding in accordance with the stages until reaching the limit of awakening and entering the state of mutual interfusion is called Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*). This sutra represents the sudden teaching of the One Vehicle, wherein the realization of the Buddha-body is suddenly perfected;
it differs from the *Śrī-mālā-devī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*, which takes only the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* as its standard.
This is because the Vajra-samādhi, the Śūraṅgama-samādhi, the Prajñāpāramitā, Nirvāṇa, and Buddha-nature are of the same essence, differing only in name.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta said, “In the realization of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), there is no coming or going;

by means of what dharma does the mind enter the limit of reality? The Buddha said, “Regarding the dharma of the limit of reality, that dharma has no limit. A mind that is itself without limit enters the limit of reality.”
The Buddha said: "The benefit of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-āśraya*) is without emergence or entry, whereas the six practices of the practitioner involve cultivation and realization;
these two are utterly inconsistent. I have not yet understood by what mental state one may enter the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*). The Buddha replied:
'I say that the benefit of original enlightenment is the essence and the cause, while the six practices are the conduct and the function. It is by means of this function [that one enters]."
To penetrate the essence is to realize the essence; when the cause is extinguished, there is neither realization nor attainment.
This state of neither realization nor attainment is a mind without boundaries, which is the meaning of entering the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); there is no other limit apart from this.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta said: "The mind of boundless wisdom has no limit; with this limitless mind, one attains mastery over the mind.

Through this mastery of wisdom, one enters the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*). Yet, as for those ordinary beings of weak minds whose hearts are full of agitation, by what dharma may they be governed so that they may attain a firm mind and enter the reality-limit?"
By means of the six practices, one enters the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). Upon entering the limit of reality, both effort and practice are forgotten;
suchness remains as it is, and the wisdom of the mind in meditative concentration is boundless. This is truly in accordance with the holy instructions.

However, if even the breath of an ordinary person’s mind makes entry into concentration difficult, how could they enter the limit of reality? I do not yet understand by what method this is governed. Generally, there are four ways for an ordinary person to cultivate *śamatha* and enter concentration.
There are four stages: first wind, second breath, third panting, and fourth respiration; only when the path of respiration becomes subtle and continuous can one enter meditative concentration.
Now, although ordinary people have abandoned wind and breath, they still possess panting and pursuit; therefore, one requests the Dharma to govern them.
The Buddha said: "As for that panting of the mind of a bodhisattva, it arises because internal and external afflictions (*kleśa*) flow and drip like a stream, forming an ocean;
when great winds stir the waves, the great dragons are terrified, and because of this terrified mind, there is much panting.

The bodhisattva causes those sentient beings to abide in the three [precepts] and guard the one [mind], entering the Tathāgata-dhyāna; by means of this meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), the mind is then without panting."
The "inner and outer messengers" refer to the fifty-one mental factors; these are the internal and external states of mind that can influence things, which constitute the Tathāgata’s mind.
When the mind follows these messengers to influence things, it is called the "drip-drip" of ordinary beings—this means accumulation.
The mind flows along with these messengers to accumulate the myriad dharmas, containing an inner ocean of the mind, just as the ocean contains the hundreds of rivers within it.
The "great wind" that contains the seeds from time immemorial within the eight consciousnesses refers to the objects of the six sense-fields (*ṣaḍviṣaya*).

The "great dragon" refers to the mind-king (*cittarāja*). Because this mind undergoes transformations with sovereign mastery, it is metaphorically likened to a dragon. Thus, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "The eight consciousnesses are like a great ocean;
the objects of the six consciousnesses are the wind, and the seventh consciousness gives rise to the waves. The meaning is the same. If one can practice accordingly...
When one ceases [distraction], after a long time the panting ceases; when the panting ceases, the path of respiration becomes subtle and continuous, and one naturally enters and abides in samādhi.
That there is no panting once one abides in samādhi is an inevitable principle.
Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva asked: "What is meant by 'preserving the three and guarding the one' to enter the Tathāgata-dhyāna? The Buddha said: "As for preserving the three:"
"To maintain the three liberations while guarding the one" means to guard the single mind as when entering the Tathāgata-dhyāna;

to contemplate the principle of the mind as when entering the stage of Suchness (Tathatā-bhūmi) is to enter the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi). The Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta asked: "What are these dharmas of the three liberations?
From what dharma does the samādhi of contemplating the principle enter? The Buddha said: "The three liberations are: liberation like empty space, liberation like gold, and liberation like water."
Regarding the contemplation of the mind according to the principle of liberation through the wisdom of liberation: the mind is pure according to that principle;
there is no "non-mind" that can be excluded. Liberation as space is the Dharma-body itself, which, like empty space, pervades the ten directions, being nowhere absent.
It has no form or segments to be apprehended, and its boundaries cannot be sought. Liberation as the vajra is the wondrous...
There is that which is like a vajra: entering into mud or water, it is not defiled or damaged.
Because the prajñā-liberation is true emptiness (*śūnyatā*) that shatters all illusory existence, these three are neither one nor three, yet they are simultaneously three and one;
therefore, they are called "inconceivable. As for "the mind is pure according to principle": this means that wisdom accords with *tathatā* (suchness) and is not subject to arising.
It is neither extinction nor existence, neither non-existence nor defilement, nor purity; it is free from all marks and is the reality of all dharmas.
This is what is meant by the severance of the path of words and the cessation of the tracks of mind and thought—exactly as the ancients said: "I have removed the place where you can apply your mind."

The Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta asked: "What is meant by 'maintaining and employing,' and how does one contemplate this? The Buddha said: "When mind and phenomena are non-dual, this is called 'maintaining and employing.
When internal practice and external practice, as well as entering and exiting, are non-dual; when the mind does not dwell on any single characteristic and is free from gain or loss;
and when the one and the many are not distinct, such that the pure mind flows into [enlightenment]—this is called 'contemplating. A Bodhisattva who is such a person does not dwell in duality."

Although he does not leave the household life nor dwell as a householder, and thus lacks the dharma-robes and does not fully maintain the *prātimokṣa* precepts or enter the *poṣadha*, he is able, through the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) freedom of his own mind, to attain the fruits of sainthood.
Without dwelling in the Two Vehicles, he enters the Bodhisattva path; thereafter, he shall fulfill the stages and realize the Bodhi of a Buddha.
Mind is principle and phenomena are objects; mind and objects are suchness (*tathatā*). This is called non-duality. Internally it is mind, externally it is objects.
To abandon phenomena and follow principle is called "entering"; to apply principle to phenomena is called "emerging. Because of suchness, there is non-duality;
because of non-duality, one eternally abides in the single mark, where there is neither attainment nor loss, yet phenomena are attained.
The principle being harmonious is called "one principle"; its transforming according to phenomena is called "not one. Whether phenomena or principle, both flow from the pure mind.

One who can cultivate contemplation in this way does not abide in dualistic characteristics—such as existence and non-existence, arising and ceasing, phenomena and principle, or defilement and purity.
Because they are non-dual, they are neither true nor conventional, but are transcendent.
Dwelling in the realm of empty space, without relying on the dharma-robes or fully maintaining the precepts, one directly enters the Bodhisattva vehicle and transcends the two vehicles.
This is called "initial-moment perfect enlightenment. The *Avataṃsaka* states that upon first generating the mind, one immediately ascends to perfect enlightenment;
the *Sāgaramati-paripṛcchā* states that although the fruit has not yet been attained, they are already sages. The meaning is the same. From Kāśyapa downward, all the great [disciples]...

The Patriarchs all resided in this land; therefore, a monk asked National Teacher Nanyang Zhong, "Does the Dharma-body realized by the Master accord with or differ from that of the Buddhas of the three periods?
The Master said, "Do you ask about the Dharma-body within the causal stage, or the Dharma-body at the stage of fruition?
[The monk] replied, "I am ignorant and deluded and do not know; I beg the Master to grant me an instruction."

The Master said: "If you ask about the Dharmakāya within the causal stage, I, this old monk, and all the elder patriarchs and Buddhas of the three periods of time are like water poured from one vessel into another—there is not even a drop lacking.
If you ask about the Dharmakāya on the level of fruition, I have not yet seen it even in my dreams.
From this point, one must give rise to faith and proceed through the ten abodes, the ten practices, the ten transferences, and up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment."
Because one ascends to wondrous enlightenment, it is said that "later, one shall fulfill the stages and attain the Bodhi of Buddhahood. People today do not recognize this stage;

they assume that upon awakening to the Way, one is immediately identical to a Buddha in fruition. They exalt the state of the sages while resigning themselves to being excluded from it. How lamentable it is that they do not immediately resolve to generate the aspiration for enlightenment!
The Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta said: "Such a person as this is inconceivable; they are neither one who has left the household life nor one who has not left it.
Why? Because they have entered the abode of nirvāṇa, donned the robes of the Tathāgata, and sat upon the seat of enlightenment.
Such a person—even if they are merely a śramaṇa—should be honored and supported."
Regarding what is called "leaving home" (renunciation), there are three types: first, the worldly household; second, the household of the triple world; and third, the household of ignorance.
Although the preceding text did not mention leaving home, it implies that one does not leave the household of the triple world or the household of ignorance.
By not dwelling in the household, one has already left the worldly household. This state—neither leaving home nor not leaving home—is what is meant by "not yet having attained."

If one is thus a sage, why is this so? It is because if one awakens to the principle of the true suchness (*tathatā*) and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), being without birth and without marks, the mind attains peace and happiness;

having already received the protection of the Tathāgata’s robe, one is not only revered by devas and humans, but even śramaṇas should respect and support such a person, as was the case with those like the Layman Pang.
Furthermore, "śramaṇa" is a general term for a follower of the Buddha.

The Buddha said: "It is thus. Why? Because one enters the abode of nirvāṇa with a mind that transcends the three realms, dons the robe of the Tathāgata, enters the sphere of the emptiness of dharmas, sits upon the seat of bodhi, and ascends to the single ground of perfect enlightenment.
For such a person, whose mind surpasses that of the two vehicles, how much more so should one respect and provide for them, even if they are merely a śramaṇa?"

The commentary on the seal explains that what was previously understood as "this mind transcending the three realms" is called entering nirvana; it does not reside in shaving the head or entering the state of the emptiness of dharmas.
What is called "donning the Buddha's robe" does not reside in wearing black robes; what is called "sitting upon the seat of enlightenment" does not reside in the site of the bodhimaṇḍa.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta said, "Is it not as if those of the two vehicles do not see that single ground and the ocean of emptiness?
The Buddha said, "It is so. Those of the two vehicles, being attached to the flavor of samādhi and having attained a body of samādhi, are like those afflicted by the malady of wine;
they remain in a state of stupor and intoxication within that single ground and the ocean of emptiness, and even after many kalpas, they still do not awaken from the wine."

Only after the initial cessation of delusions does one realize and cultivate these practices; subsequently, one attains the Buddha-body. Like that person, from the moment they abandon the state of an icchantika, they enter the six practices.

Within the stage of practice, their single thought-moment of pure mind is decisively clear and bright, possessing the diamond-like power of wisdom, the stage of non-retrogression (avaivartika), the liberation of sentient beings, and inexhaustible compassion.
That "One Ground" is the stage of initial enlightenment and the ocean of the true nature of emptiness;
it is the realm of the Great Mind, which cannot be perceived by those of the Two Vehicles.

Although the Tathāgata’s seal of understanding is not entirely absent in them, they are temporarily lost due to being intoxicated by samādhi. Once their concentration awakens and they resolve to attain enlightenment, they shall once again become Buddhas.

When the ground exists in this way, those who practice through visualization, from the moment they abandon all conceptual proliferation and give rise to a single thought of enlightenment, immediately enter the first stage of the six practices.
This is the stage of initial faith in the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), which is also the stage of Dry Wisdom (*ganhui*).
Here, wisdom is equal to that of a Buddha, yet one has not yet connected with the Tathāgata’s stream of Dharma. From this point, one sets out on foot to cultivate the six practices.
Reaching such wondrous enlightenment likewise proceeds through gradual entry; how then can it be called the "Sudden Teaching"?

This Bodhisattva of great resolve, with a single thought of pure mind, is decisively clear and possesses power equal to that of a diamond, unlike those of the three vehicles who follow a gradual mechanism.

Those on the higher stages whose afflictions remain mutually hesitant and unclear, compared to this one who, upon attaining their own benefit, immediately applies themselves—[how vast is the difference!]
Compassion that universally delivers sentient beings is what distinguishes [the Bodhisattva path] from the Two Vehicles.
The Bodhisattva Mahābala said: "Such a person should not uphold the precepts; they should not revere the śramaṇas. The Buddha said:

"To speak of the precepts for them is due to unwholesome pride and because they are like the waves of the ocean. It is as described in the eighth chapter of the *Cittabhūmi* (The Ground of the Mind)."
The ocean of consciousness is clear and the nine consciousnesses flow in purity; the wind cannot move it and waves do not arise.

The nature of the precepts is equal to emptiness, yet those who hold to them are deluded and inverted like that person. When the seven and six [consciousnesses] do not arise, all accumulations cease in meditative concentration. Without departing from the three Buddhas, one gives rise to bodhicitta.
Within the three marks of non-existence, one follows the mind and enters the profound mystery, deeply revering the Triple Gem and never losing dignified deportment.

That śramaṇa is not without reverence for bodhisattvas; that noble one does not abide in the mundane dharmas of movement or non-movement, enters the three assemblies of emptiness, and extinguishes the three types of existence.

While the two vehicles maintain the precepts of observance and violation, of action and cessation, the Mahāyāna does not "maintain" them—this is not called a failure to maintain the nature-precepts (dharmatā-śīla).
Furthermore, Śramaṇas do not revere the inner seal of equality, nor do they revere the Goddess of Merit (Puṇyadevatā), nor do they loathe the Woman of Darkness (Tamasī);
both are abandoned by them. The Buddha replied: "Those who speak of precepts truly have no precepts to speak of.
Because sentient beings possess the ten unwholesome paths of action, I teach them to abandon the unwholesome and cultivate the wholesome; yet there are various forms of pride."
Therefore, I exhort them to abandon arrogance and cultivate humility and respect.

Since the mind and consciousness are turbulent like the waves of a great ocean, one should practice the restraint of the precepts (*śīla-saṃvara*) to still that agitation and abide in purity; thus it is said that maintaining the precepts is like [stabilizing] their function.
When one contemplates and cultivates the eight consciousnesses until the ocean is clear and no longer moved by the eight winds, what further need is there to maintain the precepts? VIII.
Consciousness is the mind; the nine consciousnesses are the nature; the waves are the seven consciousnesses; and the wind is the six sense objects.

When these seven and six do not arise, one has already entered the samādhi of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*). Although there is no further need for cessation, one does not remain in the samādhi of cessation, because one extensively performs the deeds of a Buddha.
Thus, without departing from Buddhahood, one generates the bodhicitta, which is signless and unimpeded.
Within the state of the Middle Way mind that transcends all marks, one enters in accordance with the fact that the Three Jewels are of one essence;
thus, although there is nothing to be revered, this does not contradict the act of reverence.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta said: "O virtuous one, you have indeed fulfilled the perfections; you are the Tathāgata-garbha, the very form of the Buddha."
Thus, in the presence of the Buddha, he generates the bodhicitta and enters the threefold pure precepts;

he does not dwell in their characteristics, extinguishes the three types of existence, does not abide in the state of quiescence, and does not abandon the assembly of the worthy, entering the inconceivable stage of non-discipline.
When one can thus maintain the application and cultivate contemplation within a single thought-moment, it is called the fulfillment of the fruit;

for by being able to accord with the three Buddhas, the Buddha of Sufficient Virtue is the Sambhogakāya (Enjoyment Body), the Buddha of the Tathāgatagarbha is the Dharmakāya (Dharma Body), and the Buddha of the Image is the Nirmāṇakāya (Response Body).
These three Buddhas are perfectly manifested in a single thought-moment, and the arousal of the bodhicitta is an indestructible transformation.

Because he maintains the threefold discipline according to ritual, he does not violate the Dharma-body; because he is unattached to phenomena, he extinguishes the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*).

Thus, he does not abide in the mundane world, nor does he dwell in a state of quiescence; he does not abide in the supramundane world, for his response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is like an illusion or a transformation.
Because he does not destroy compassion, there are those with the capacity to be saved.

Teaching the Dharma according to what is appropriate, those who are not yet disciplined find no discipline; this state of non-discipline is precisely the practice of effortlessness (*anābhoga*), which is not a realm conceivable by the three vehicles.
At that time, Śāriputra rose from his seat, stepped forward, and spoke these verses:
The Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta asked: "Why did Śāriputra speak these verses? It is because this chapter is titled "Entering the Reality-limit" (*bhūtakoṭi-praveśa*).
Since a bodhisattva has already entered the stage of the reality-limit, there is nothing further to be praised;
therefore, Śāriputra—a person of the two vehicles—is employed to represent the second gate of meaning. This is also called "indirect praise. Why is it that those of the two vehicles are so numerous?
Śāriputra alone praised him, saying: "Is there not a profound intention here? This principle of ultimate reality cannot be even faintly approximated except through wisdom.
Possessing the full ocean of *prajñā*, he does not dwell in the city of *nirvāṇa*, like that wondrous lotus flower."
The high plateau is not the place from which they emerge; It is through immeasurable kalpas that the Buddhas attain it.
Without abandoning the various afflictions, one cannot cross over to the world beyond; It is like a lotus emerging from the mud.
It is as practiced by Bodhisattvas on the six stages of action, And like those three clusters of emptiness— Such is the true path of Bodhi.
I now abide in non-abiding, as the Buddha has taught: having come, one returns again;

only when fully perfected does one emerge. Furthermore, I cause all sentient beings—those who have come before and those who will come after—to be like me, without duality, and to all attain perfect enlightenment.

Prajñāpāramitā is not Prajñāpāramitā; it is called "Prajñāpāramitā" because it perfectly and completely illuminates through the mutual integration of the three truths and the three objects, being neither partial nor biased.
This describes the meaning of perfect integration discussed in this chapter. Because of this perfect integration, one does not abide in saṃsāra, nor does one abide in nirvāṇa.
Not abiding in either extreme, yet not seeking nirvana apart from saṃsāra— saṃsāra itself is nirvana—
one does not dwell in saṃsāra while remaining unimpeded in taking birth and undergoing death to deliver all sentient beings; nor does one dwell in nirvana,
for one constantly experiences peace and bliss, untainted by afflictions, and is thus like a wondrous lotus.
The lotus flower is defiled yet pure; likewise, this perfectly integrated wisdom is not possessed by those of the Two Vehicles, just as the lotus does not grow on high ground.
Nevertheless, these Buddhas do not attain this wisdom in a mere moment;
rather, throughout immeasurable kalpas, they do not abandon afflictions until they have delivered all sentient beings in the world, and only then do they attain it, just like that mud.
The "Flower" chapter uses the Dharma to correspond with the metaphor; here, the metaphor corresponds to the practice.

Regarding what constitutes the practice of a Bodhisattva who delivers the world, the explanation states: these six practices are precisely that which is practiced; the six practices constitute the practice.
Regarding what constitutes the attainment of the Way, those three emptinesses are the Way. The Tathāgata cultivated and trained in these six practices and three emptinesses throughout kalpas.
I, too, shall dwell in birth-and-death as the Buddha vowed, rather than dwelling in nirvana;

through one lifetime or even immeasurable lifetimes, I shall come to this world to transform and benefit sentient beings until wisdom is perfected, and only then shall I myself emerge from the triple world.
I make this vow so that every single sentient being throughout the entire dharma-realm may likewise share this same aspiration.
Those who came before and those who followed all attained perfect enlightenment.
At that time, the Buddha said to Śāriputra: "Inconceivable! You shall later achieve the path of Bodhi, and immeasurable sentient beings shall transcend the ocean of birth and death.
At that moment, the great assembly all awakened to Bodhi, as did the various groups of lesser beings.
Entering the Ocean of the Five Emptinesses.
Chapter Six: The Emptiness of True Nature.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying: "O Venerable One, when practicing the Bodhisattva path, there are no names or marks."

Regarding the lack of formal ritual in the precepts, how should one embrace them and teach them for the sake of sentient beings? I pray that the Buddha, out of his great compassion, will explain this for me.
The Buddha said: "Good son, listen attentively now; I shall explain it for you. Good son, wholesome and unwholesome dharmas are produced from the transformation of the mind.
All objective realms arise from the conceptualization of mental discourse. If one restrains these within a single point, all conditions will be severed and extinguished. Why is this so?
Therefore, son of good family, when the single root does not arise, the three functions have no place to abide; when one dwells in accordance with suchness, the gates of the six realms are closed;
when the four conditions are stilled, the three precepts are fully perfected.
Śāriputra, foremost in wisdom, understood the meaning of the true nature of emptiness upon hearing it but once;

within that emptiness of nature, he realized that on the bodhisattva path there is neither name nor mark. Previously, it was stated that the six practices are what the bodhisattva performs and the three emptinesses are what the bodhisattva realizes.
Thus, one attains the signless (*animitta*), which has two meanings: first, the dharma realized by oneself.

Because it is unattainable, it is signless (*animitta*); because two things do not communicate with one another, and because the afflictions of the upper and lower stages do not know each other, it is signless.
Since the Path is without name or sign, how could the precepts have any real ritual form?
If there is no ritual standard to rely upon, by what means will you convert and subdue sentient beings? The Buddha replied: "In truth, no name, sign, or fixed ritual can be found."

All wholesome and unwholesome phenomena are established through the illusory projections of one’s own mind. If one can realize that the mind has no intrinsic existence, then there will be neither names nor signs.
If one cannot thus awaken to the nature of the mind, then one observes the conceptualization of thought and speech.
Why is this? Because there are no phenomena external to the mind; phenomena arise from the mind. The arising of phenomena from the mind first proceeds through a single moment of thought and speech.

Since external objects do not arise, what form could they have? Therefore it is said: "When one is concentrated in a single place, all conditions are severed. There are two aspects to this "single place":
first, taking the True as the object, wherein the mind is released into the unconditioned and cultivates *śamatha* (calm abiding) in a single flavor;

regarding this, Tiantai speaks of "stopping by taking the true nature as the object" (*tǐzhēn zhǐ*), which involves many kinds of distinctions, as detailed in the *Zhìguān* (Mohe Zhiguan). Second, taking the conventional as the object, wherein one recollects the Buddha’s name with focused mindfulness. Or...

Because one upholds mantras and recites sutras, it is said: "If one concentrates on a single point, there is no task that cannot be accomplished. When practicing *śamatha* (calm abiding), there is nothing upon which to rest;
by taking the Buddha as the object, there is nothing to be thought of. When there is no-thought (*amanasikāra*), one does not calculate existence or non-existence.
When there is no resting, discrimination does not arise. When there is no discrimination, even "one" has no name; how then could there be "three"? How could there be "one," "three," or "ten"?

When there is no discrimination, one eternally abides in True Suchness; because one abides in True Suchness, the gates to the six realms are closed and the three functions cease—this refers precisely to emptiness, the provisional, and the middle.
This answers the meaning of the Bodhisattva path being without names or marks.
Śāriputra asked, "What are the four conditions by which one fully possesses the three types of precepts? The Buddha said, "The four conditions are:

first, the power of performing analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), which comprises the *saṃvara-śīla* (precept of restraint); second, the power of the fundamental benefit of purified faculties, which gives rise to the *kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla* (precept of gathering virtuous dharmas);
third, the power of fundamental wisdom and great compassion, which comprises the *sattva-anugrāhaka-śīla* (precept of benefiting sentient beings); fourth, [is]..."
The power of the wisdom of universal awakening takes as its object that which accords with abiding in suchness; this is called the four conditions.

Good son, in this way, the power of the four great conditions does not abide in the characteristics of phenomena, yet it is not without functional efficacy; it cannot be sought apart from a single locus.
Good son, in this way, a single matter universally encompasses the six practices; this is the Buddha’s bodhi, the ocean of sarvajñā.

"Action" refers to that which is performed; because taking precepts as action constitutes its essential nature, "discernment" means the discernment of what is wholesome—such as "this should be done" and "this should not be done.
Through the power of such discernment, one abandons evil; with this function as a condition, restraint is established through the practice of cessation and maintenance.

It receives its name by being contrasted with the commission of faults. As for the inclusion of virtue, it relies upon the fundamental practices of a bodhisattva and does not require [external] effort.
For a Bodhisattva who takes the accumulation of merit through a single flavor of roots of goodness as the causal basis for wisdom, this fundamental wisdom is attained without contrivance;
such is the virtue of self-benefit. Once self-benefit is complete, one must further benefit others by universally mobilizing great compassion to deliver sentient beings.
If one does not deliver sentient beings, one falls into the path of the Two Vehicles and becomes a solitary awakened one (pratyekabuddha).
That which is original enlightenment is itself the Middle Way; the Dharmakāya’s supernatural powers emerging into the provisional is itself the wisdom of liberation;
that which illuminates illusory existence is itself Prajñā. These three accord with Suchness and abide in its functioning, answering the three precepts.

The first two phrases are specific, while this one phrase is general; the general and specific encompass one another, not departing from the mind itself, which is the condition of the four great elements.
The designations used to express persons are not without their names, yet the ultimate reality (bhūtakoṭi) is fundamentally without marks (animitta), because it does not abide in phenomena.
Nevertheless, because its functioning is perfectly clear even while not abiding in phenomena, it is said that "the glue and blue are within the color" and "the salty taste is within the water.
If one seeks names and marks apart from one's own mind, they cannot be found at all; a single phenomenon encompasses all six.
The practitioner thus single-mindedly fulfills the six stages; how could it stop at merely these six practices?

Since both wholesome and unwholesome dharmas are manifested from the mind, what is there—whether mundane or supramundane—that is not encompassed? These six practices are the cause, and Sarvajña (omniscience) is the fruit.
The cause encompasses the ocean of the fruit, and the fruit reaches back to the source of the cause. Has there ever been anything outside of one’s own mind?
Śāriputra said: "Not dwelling on the characteristics of phenomena, yet not being without effort—this is the true emptiness of dharmas, eternal, blissful, self, and pure;
it transcends the two kinds of self and is Great Parinirvāṇa. This mind is unattached; this is the contemplation of great power.
Within the awakening of this contemplation, one should fully possess the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment."
"Not abiding in the characteristics of phenomena" means not being attached to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). "Not lacking in effort" means not being obstructed by the conditioned.
Not being attached to the conditioned is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); not being obstructed by the conditioned is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

Since the two truths are non-dual, they take the dharma-nature of true emptiness as their essence, functioning in perfect fusion and simultaneous operation. Because they operate simultaneously, the four virtues are accomplished.
Transcending the two selves, one realizes the mind of great peace and bliss, yet does not even cling to that peace and bliss; this is the "Contemplation of Great Power.

This contemplation is precisely that which was asked about by the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta; it should be understood as the complete path of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) that is spontaneously accomplished without effort.

The Buddha said: "It is so. One who is fully endowed with the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment—namely, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path—possesses these many names for a single meaning.
They are neither identical nor different; they are merely names and mere syllables. Since phenomena (*dharma*) cannot be apprehended, that which is unapprehendable is one."
Meaning is without words, and words lack the characteristics of meaning; the true nature of reality is emptiness, and the meaning of emptiness is suchness as it truly is.
The principle of suchness encompasses all phenomena. Noble son, those who abide in accordance with this principle transcend the ocean of the three sufferings.

The Buddha said: "It is so. These dharmas that comprise the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma) are called 'factors of enlightenment' because, although their names are many, their meaning is but one mind.
Since the mind has no dual function, they are not different; since their sequential order is not fixed, they are not one.
When expressed through words and letters, there are thirty-seven numbers, but in the ultimate reality, these dharmas cannot be apprehended. Why is this?"
Within the attainment of the true nature of emptiness (tathatā-śūnyatā), there is neither word nor meaning;

because there are no words, the path of verbal expression is severed, and because there is no meaning, it is called the emptiness of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-śūnyatā). Yet, both words and meanings flow forth from within the nature of true emptiness;
since the true nature is suchness (tathatā), it possesses all phenomena through that very suchness.

Śāriputra said: "If all phenomena are entirely characterized by words and language, and these characteristics are not themselves the meaning—since the meaning as it truly is cannot be expressed in words—how then does the Tathāgata now preach the Dharma?"
As the Buddha has taught that words are not the meaning and that the true meaning is ineffable, I do not yet understand, World-Honored One, by what means you preach the Dharma.

If you were to speak solely in accordance with ultimate reality, you should remain perpetually silent; if you were to speak solely through skillful means and conceptual distinctions, you would fall into the trap of words and meanings.
Since it is difficult to find conviction in either of these two dilemmas, I ask this question.
The Buddha said: "When I preach the Dharma, it is because you sentient beings speak of birth; therefore, I speak of that which cannot be spoken, and thus I preach it.
What I have preached is speech of meaning, not speech of words; what sentient beings speak is speech of words, not speech of meaning.

That which is not speech of meaning is entirely empty and non-existent. The phrase 'empty and non-existent' is itself wordless. To be wordless regarding meaning is to not speak of meaning at all—and all such things are [ultimately] so."
False speech is like speech according to reality: it is empty yet not empty, real yet not real, free from the two marks.

It does not abide in the middle, nor is it the dharma of non-middle; it is free from the three marks. No locus is perceived. Suchness is as it is spoken: as there is no "is," there is no "is-not"; as there is no "is-not," there is no "is-not-is-not"; as there is no "is-not-is-not," there is no "is. As for "is," "is" is not present in speech.
It neither exists nor does not exist; it is as it is (tathatā), yet there is no "as-it-is-ness" that can be said to exist or not exist.

The Dharma is fundamentally beyond expression, yet because sentient beings dwell within the cycle of birth and death and are unable to transcend it, the Buddha employs skillful means to speak within that which is inexpressible.
The meaning spoken by the Buddha is not found in the literal words; it is like a person who has actually arrived at their destination.
That which is described in Beijing is all truly what sentient beings have spoken;
as for words that lack meaning, such as those heard by chance on the road or passed down through hearsay, whatever is so spoken is entirely false because it has not reached its source.
Since the meaning of what the Buddha has taught differs from worldly speech, what real meaning could there be in the assertions of non-Buddhists? Thus, they are severed.
That which is constantly mixed with these is called "proliferation" (*prapañca*), spoken by ordinary worldlings who know only the mundane and do not believe in the supramundane;
this is called "falsehood. That which is spoken by the Three Vehicles, wherein gains and losses mutually arise, is merely called "expedient means" (*upāya*).

However, the Buddha’s teaching is that emptiness is neither empty nor non-empty; non-emptiness is immediately emptiness. Reality is neither real nor unreal; non-reality is neither existence nor non-existence.
Non-existence itself is precisely the Middle Way, yet even this "Middle" is not the Middle; because one does not cling to these three, there is no location.
Since there is no location, how can one speak of *tathatā* (suchness)?

One speaks of it because *bhūtatathatā* (true suchness) does not belong to words, does not belong to language, does not involve existence or non-existence, does not calculate gain or loss, and does not cling to the ordinary or the holy.
Therefore, the subsequent statements are likewise so. The meaning of these following sentences is that within True Suchness (tathatā) there are no names of relative opposition;
because of the presence of such opposition between existence and non-existence, one speaks of the "non-existence" of non-existence to remedy it.
Once both existence and non-existence have departed, there is no longer any [clinging] to non-existence. While within True Suchness there is no "non-existence," True Suchness itself exists.

Furthermore, because there are no sentient beings who cling to the two extremes and thus wander through birth and death, the Buddha taught the Dharma so that they would not abide in those two extremes.
He spoke of the Middle Way, which is suchness (tathatā) that is ultimately beyond words; yet even this suchness does not exist.
Nevertheless, for the sake of delivering sentient beings, it is not non-existent, as has been explained.
Śāriputra asked: "From the icchantika up to the icchantika-mind, in what stage do all sentient beings abide so as to attain the Tathāgata and the true reality (tathatā) of the Tathāgata?
The Buddha said: "From the icchantika-mind up to the Tathāgata and the true reality of the Tathāgata, they abide in five stages.
The first is the stage of faith (śraddhā-bhūmi), wherein one believes that the seed of *tathatā* within this body is obscured by delusion."

Having cast off that which obscures, one abandons the deluded mind; the pure mind is pristine white, knowing all objective realms as being the dualistic conceptualization of mental discourse (*manojalpa-vikalpa*).

Second is the stage of reflection (*cintā-avasthā*); "reflection" means contemplating that all objective realms are merely mental discourse and conceptualizations of mental discourse, appearing according to the mind.

The perceived objects are not my own fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*); one knows this fundamental consciousness to be neither phenomena (*dharma*) nor objects (*artha*), neither the grasped (*grāhya*) nor...

First, regarding the three types of practitioners in the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-avasthā*): the practitioner constantly gives rise to [the path]; that which gives rise [to it] and the act of giving rise occur simultaneously;

first, guided by wisdom, they eliminate all obstacles and difficulties, emerging from the fetters of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*). Fourth, regarding the practitioner in the stage of practice (*caryā-avasthā*): having departed from the stages of conditioned activity (*saṃskāra-bhūmi*), their mind is free from grasping or rejecting;
their faculties are utterly pure and sharp, and their mind is immovable, like the definitive true nature (*tattva-svabhāva*) of Great Parinirvāṇa, which is solely the ultimate nature (*dharmatā*).

Regarding the five stages of the Great Emptiness (*ākāśa-mahābhūta*): "Abandoning" means abandoning positions; "abandoning" means not abiding in nature. It is the flow of the correct wisdom of emptiness, which is easily transformed into great compassion.
Its characteristics do not abide in suchness (*tathatā*). Like *samyak-saṃbodhi*, it is a mind of non-attainment;

the mind has no boundaries and no place where it can be seen. This is reaching the stage of the Tathāgata. Son of good family, these five stages are: first, awakening; entering from the fundamental benefit; and if one transforms sentient beings.

From its original state—wherein the term *icchantika* in Sanskrit means "one who lacks faith"—from the moment one lacks faith until the very instant they resolve their mind toward awakening (*cittotpāda*), they abandon the state of an *icchantika*.
Within this interval, through what stages do they pass to reach the stage of a Tathāgata? The Buddha said: There are.
Regarding the five kinds of faith: faith is the source of the Way and the mother of all merit, for it nurtures all roots of goodness;

therefore, faith must take the lead. There are ten types of faith, which, when summarized, do not go beyond these: first, one must have faith that within one's own body there exists the seed of *tathatā* (suchness).
Although this seed exists, it cannot manifest because it is obstructed by delusion. Furthermore, one must have faith...
That which is obstructed is not caused by another, but arises entirely from one's own mental verbalization (*manojalpa-vikalpa*).
If one realizes that the objects of mental verbalization are empty, what need is there for conceptual thought? Thus, those at the stage of faith within the Ten Abodes generate faith through hearing;

conceptual thought gives rise to understanding through reflection, and this understanding knows that all objects arise solely from mental verbalization and are not the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*). Why is this so? Because within the fundamental consciousness...
That which is non-dharma is neither words nor meaning; since both words and meaning are absent, how could there be anything to be grasped or rejected?

For the practitioner, this refers to the ten practices (*daśabhūmi*). Through understanding, one initiates practice; through initiating practice, one gives rise to the mind of cultivation. Mind and contemplation arise simultaneously.
When contemplation can destroy delusion, delusion is destroyed and wisdom is born. When wisdom is born, one emerges from obstructions and leaves behind the veils. Thus it is for the practitioner.
This refers to the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*), which turn oneself toward others because one does not seek for oneself;

and the stage of "leaving all formations" (*sarvasaṃskāra-prahāṇa-bhūmi*), where one's own practice is already perfected. "Immovable and certain relinquishment" refers to the relinquishment of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

Relinquishing the mundane means not abiding in existence (*bhava*); relinquishing the supramundane means not abiding in emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Both emptiness and existence flow forth from right wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*).

To harmonize the existence, non-existence, and transformation of sentient beings so that each is suited to their capacity and none are left empty-handed or discarded—this is called great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).

It is called "great" because it is unconditioned compassion (*apratihata-karuṇā*) that regards all beings with equality, making no distinction between enemies and kin, never giving rise to attachment or views, and always conforming to the true nature (*tathatā*). If one gives rise to the notion of being a "savior," [one is not truly great].

Its characteristics do not correspond to *tathatā* (suchness), yet although it is eternally non-deviant from suchness, for the sake of delivering sentient beings, one maintains a mind of emptiness toward *samyaksambodhi* (perfect enlightenment) and does not realize it.
Why does one not realize it? Because the Bodhisattva’s mental scope is boundless, vowing never to abandon even a single sentient being;
thus, one does not perceive a location where there is a cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) to be abandoned, nor does one perceive [a place] where there is...
Nirvana is thus realized through such practice; this is the attainment of the Tathāgata. Regarding the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the Tathāgata:
the "upper" Tathāgata is the Buddha of Retribution (*vipākaphala-buddha*), while the "lower" Tathāgata is the Buddha of Ultimate Realization (*niṣṭhā-gata-buddha*).

Good son, although five [bodies] are spoken of, they all enter by means of inverse contemplation into the self-nature of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-ādi-bodhi*), and are not obtained from without. This is for the purpose of transforming sentient beings.
"One should establish designations based on one's own realization.
Śāriputra asked, "How does one proceed from its original place? The Buddha said, "It has been without an original place from the very beginning.
By entering into the reality of the sphere of emptiness where there is no place, one gives rise to the Bodhicitta and brings the holy path to fulfillment. Why is this? Good son, it is like..."
Grasping at that emptiness with the hand, one neither attains it nor fails to attain it.
Since there is originally no foundation, the mind does not know itself; abiding in a placeless state, the Way has no location.

Taking emptiness as the object of focus, one enters reality; entering reality, one is neither empty nor non-empty. Simultaneously negating and simultaneously illuminating—this is called "fulfillment."
The Noble Path is neither "unattainable" nor "not unattainable. This is intended as an analogy for entering reality through the realm of space (*ākāśa*):
because space cannot be grasped, it is said to be "unattainable"; yet, when one grasps at space with the hand, there is already the "space of a fist," hence it is said to be "not unattainable.

This is used as a metaphor for the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*): since [the nature] is fundamentally complete and lacks any portion that can be acquired, it is called "unattainable" due to adventitious [defilements].
Because one severs hindrances and emerges from entanglements due to the removal of the dust-obstructions, one realizes bodhi;

thus it is said that it is not that one does not attain it. Śāriputra said: "As the Venerable One has explained, taking the fundamental benefit prior to the manifestation of phenomena, this mindfulness is quiescent.
Quiescence is suchness (*tathatā*). It encompasses all virtues and integrates all dharmas; it is non-dual and inconceivable."
You should know that this Dharma is the Mahāprajñāpāramitā; it is the great divine mantra, the great illuminating mantra, the unsurpassed mantra, and the mantra equal to the unequaled.

That which exists prior to all things is the state before even a single thought has arisen. This non-arising of a single thought is precisely the wondrous luminosity of original enlightenment (*mūla-avabodha*), naturally and spontaneously functioning.
In a single kṣaṇa, no characteristic of arising can be apprehended; in a single kṣaṇa, no characteristic of cessation can be apprehended.
This is quiescent extinction (*śānti-nirodha*). This very quiescent extinction is the meaning of True Suchness (*tathatā*); because it is suchness, it is able to...

The dhāraṇī that encompasses all myriad virtues is the meaning of quiescent extinction, which is neither arising nor ceasing. Although it is without arising or ceasing, it does not obstruct the blazing process of arising and ceasing;
this is what is called the inconceivable. One who can understand this true emptiness is Mahāprajñāpāramitā.
For one who understands this, a single thought-moment can transcend all obstacles—this is the Great Divine Mantra.
It is a great vidyā-mantra capable of shattering the long night of all ignorance; its true nature is the principle of emptiness, which only a Buddha can realize.
It is the unsurpassed mantra, peerless among both mundane and supramundane things; it is the mantra of the unequaled.
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is. The fire of wisdom—true suchness, emptiness, and the emptiness of nature—burns away all fetters, rendering them equal and perfectly equal.
In the three stages of wondrous enlightenment, the three bodies are brilliantly clear and pure within the nine consciousnesses, devoid of any shadows.
Good son, this Dharma is neither cause nor condition; because wisdom functions autonomously, its activity is neither moving nor still."

Because its nature is empty, it is neither existent nor non-existent; because the mark of emptiness itself is empty, O son of good family, if one transforms sentient beings and causes them to contemplate and enter into this meaning, those who enter into this meaning see the Tathāgata.
The Buddha verified these two points as follows: first, he sealed his attainment of mindfulness prior to the [attainment of] realization;

second, he sealed his ability to maintain all myriad virtues through total retention (*dhāraṇī*). When one attains the essential meaning, all fetters and outflows are incinerated in a single thought-moment, and all phenomena proceed toward the true emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
This "proceeding" is not a passing over; it is known that true emptiness is precisely within the state of equality.
That which is most equal, though it is true emptiness, nonetheless contains all myriad virtues; there is nothing that does not flow into and reach the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*).

Viewed from the preceding stages, these are the stages of sequential practice (*xingbu*); from the first ground (*bhūmi*) up to the tenth, the intermediate stage is precisely the Ground of Equal Enlightenment.
Viewed from the subsequent stages, this is the Ground of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*). Therefore, it is said: "Reaching equality."
Having awakened, one attains the Vajra Mind; this is the initial stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*).
The wondrous awakening of the three bodies—Dharmakāya, Saṃbhogakāya, and Nirmāṇakāya—is such that these three are one and one is three, perfectly interfused and sovereign;

thus it is called "wondrous. The ninth consciousness is named the White-Pure Consciousness (*viśuddha-vijñāna*), which is another name for True Emptiness (*tathatā-śūnyatā*); having attained the essential meaning, one recalls what preceded it.
It then accords with true emptiness; within this accord, whether cause or fruit, all things are luminously pure and clear, without a single shadow of delusive thought.
This "Dharma" refers to the ninth, the white-pure consciousness (*amala-vijñāna*), which is the fundamental nature not subject to causes and conditions, being thus from the beginning.
Within this, fundamental wisdom functions spontaneously and naturally.

It is neither moving nor still; why is it neither moving nor still? Because wisdom relies upon the manifestation of the essence, and since the essence is empty, its functioning is eternally quiescent.
Being eternally quiescent, it cannot be reached by existence or non-existence.

To deliver sentient beings, it is provisionally designated as "emptiness," yet when spoken of in accordance with the nature of reality, even emptiness cannot be apprehended. Previously, Śāriputra asked about the three precepts.

Regarding how one who lacks formal ritual conduct (*anīryāpatha*) gathers in sentient beings, it is stated therein: "If one transforms sentient beings, one causes them to contemplate and enter into this meaning.
Śāriputra said: "The Tathāgata’s contemplation of this meaning does not abide within the various flows; he should transcend the four dhyānas and go beyond the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*)."

"Stream" (*srotas*) refers to categories; there are four such categories: namely, the stream of ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), the stream of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), the stream of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), and the stream of the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*).
Among these, "not abiding in any streams" means not abiding in the streams of ordinary persons or non-Buddhists;
"one who should transcend the four dhyānas" means not abiding in the stream of the two vehicles, but rather transcending the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) to enter the stream of the Great Vehicle.
The Buddha said: "It is thus. Why? Because all dharmas are merely names and numbers; the four dhyānas are also like this.

If one sees the Tathāgata, the Tathāgata’s mind is sovereign and always abides in the state of cessation (nirodha); he neither emerges nor enters, because he is equal regarding the internal and external.

Son of good family, those various dhyāna-observations are all for the sake of the concentration on emptiness of perception (saṃjñā-śūnyatā-samādhi). This is the Suchness (tathatā), not that [prior state] again."

Why is this? Because when one contemplates suchness as it truly is, one does not perceive the characteristics of contemplating suchness; all characteristics have already ceased. This cessation is the meaning of suchness.
As for that conceptualization of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), it is movement and not true concentration. Why is this? Because the nature of concentration is free from all movement;
it is neither defiled nor subject to defilement, neither a phenomenon (*dharma*) nor a reflection, and it is free from all discrimination because it is the fundamental meaning of meaning. Good son...
When one contemplates in this manner, such concentration is truly called dhyāna.
All dharmas possessed by ordinary people and non-Buddhists are merely names without meaning; even the sequential concentrations of the four dhyānas are merely names without meaning.
Therefore, when one enters the contemplation of the meaning of the Tathāgata’s original enlightenment, there is only meaning and no names.
In the ultimate sense (*tattvārtha*), because non-meaning is itself the meaning, the mind is eternally sovereign. Why is it sovereign? Because it abides in quiescence (*śānti*).
That which is called "quiescence" means that in a single moment (*kṣaṇa*) no characteristic of arising can be apprehended, and in a single moment no characteristic of cessation can be apprehended.
Since neither arising nor cessation can be apprehended, arising is not termed "emergence" and cessation is not termed "entry."
Furthermore, the meditative concentrations attained by ordinary beings involve emergence and entry, as they are all established through conceptual construction;

thus, they do not equal the Tathāgata’s concentration on the reality of things as they truly are. Why is this so? Because one contemplates reality through reality itself, and therein one does not perceive a subject that contemplates nor an object that is contemplated.
Why is nothing seen? Because within the characteristic of reality (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa*), all characteristics are entirely absent.
Regarding "quiescence" (śānti), that which is called quiescence is the meaning of reality as it is (yathābhūta).

The meditative absorption (dhyāna) established by ordinary beings through their deluded thoughts has both entering and emerging, and thus possesses movement and stillness; having both movement and stillness, it is collectively termed "deluded thought" and does not accord with "true dhyāna.
The nature of dhyāna is equal to empty space, and just as empty space has neither movement nor stillness, so too the nature of dhyāna is without movement.
Quiescence is like empty space, being neither defiled nor pure; thus, the nature of dhyāna is neither defiled nor pure.

Because the essence of empty space is not a collection of manifold forms, it is not a phenomenon; yet because it does not obstruct the manifestation of the myriad phenomena, it is not a mere reflection.

Since empty space is without discrimination, the nature of dhyāna is likewise without discrimination. Question: There is no such passage in the sūtras; why then do you use empty space as an analogy for dhyāna?
"Is this not merely a speculative assertion? He replied: "That which is said to be 'in accordance with reality' cannot be easily illustrated by the analogy of empty space;
yet sūtras such as the *Nirvāṇa* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* frequently employ empty space as a metaphor."
Śāriputra said: "The Tathāgata always transforms sentient beings through that which is truly as it is;
such a reality is characterized by many texts and vast meanings, and can only be cultivated by those with sharp faculties. It is difficult for those with dull faculties to apply their minds to it.
By what skillful means can those of dull faculties be led to enter this truth?"
That which is "as it truly is" (yathābhūta) is the fundamental awakening of sentient beings, the wondrous mind, the ground of ultimate reality (bhūtakoṭi).
This is what was referred to in the preceding text as the "meaning of singular awakening" and the "truth of the single reality. The *Lotus Sūtra* states: "This alone is the one true matter;
the other two are not real. It is also called the "one great cause and condition" (ekamahā-kārya-hetu-pratyaya), for this is the original intent of all Buddhas.
In the Hall of Universal Radiance, the Buddha suddenly expounded the Single Vehicle (Ekayāna);

because the great śrāvakas did not believe or understand it, the Tathāgata concealed the ultimate reality and established provisional means, taking the Single Vehicle and teaching it as immeasurable vehicles.

This is the bodhisattva’s task—knowing that within the words of the one true reality are fully contained manifold expressions and vast meanings—and it is not something that those of dull faculties can reach in the future.
In this age, those of sharp faculties are few; for the most part, they are of dull faculties. How, then, does the World-Honored One employ skillful means?
The Buddha said: He causes those of dull faculties to receive and uphold even a single four-line verse, whereby they immediately enter the True Reality (*bhūtārtha*).
All the Buddha-dharma is subsumed within a single four-line verse.

When expedient means are employed, the nature is manifested through many texts and vast meanings; yet when entering the reality, the path of words and thought is severed, and not even a single character can be found.
If one can believe in this Dharma as it truly is, then by upholding a single four-line verse, one may enter [the truth].
It is like tasting a single morsel from a precious cauldron and already possessing all its flavors, or drinking a single drop of the great ocean and [thereby knowing its taste].
"Since the hundred rivers possess their flavor, why must one exhaust one's mind and strength to trace their currents to their source before it can be called 'attainment'?
Śāriputra said: 'How is it that a single four-line verse [can be so]? I pray you will explain it for me. Thereupon, the Venerable One spoke these verses:"

The meaning of that which is produced by causes and conditions is that this meaning is cessation, not production. The meaning of the cessation of all arising and ceasing is that this meaning is production, not cessation.
When Śāriputra was first practicing the path of the Brahmins, he encountered Aśvajit on the road and asked him: "What does your teacher constantly teach?"
Dharmavijaya replied with a verse: "Phenomena arise from causes and conditions; Meanings cease through causes and conditions. Arising and ceasing are themselves dependent origination;
Their intrinsic nature is neither arising nor ceasing. Upon hearing this verse, Śāriputra suddenly attained enlightenment and went to take refuge in the Buddha.
This verse differs from the previous one only in its phrasing; for the phenomena produced by causes and conditions are precisely what is meant by "meaning."

"Conditioned phenomena arise and cease; when one realizes that conditioned phenomena lack intrinsic nature, then all arising and ceasing are extinguished, and self-nature is neither arising nor ceasing, eternally abiding and unchanging.
Śāriputra first attained realization of the Way through this single verse, yet he thought there must be some other further meaning.
When the World-Honored One repeated this verse at the very end, Śāriputra then knew [the Buddha's true intent].
Since the Dharma is from beginning to end without dual meaning, why should it be taught exclusively for those of dull faculties?
Even Śāriputra, though of sharp faculties, attained realization through a single verse. I truly believe what Linji said: "The Buddha-dharma is not much."

At that time, when the great assembly heard these verses, they were all filled with immense joy; they all attained the ocean of wisdom of the emptiness of nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*) which extinguishes arising and ceasing.
Having extinguished arising and ceasing, they attained non-arising (*anutpāda*). Since there is nothing that does not arise within non-arising, Prajñā manifests.
The preceding "emptiness of nature" (prakṛti-śūnyatā) is the essence, which is the meaning of non-arising; the "ocean of wisdom" is the function, which is the meaning of *prajñā*.
Because of the emptiness of nature, although the myriad phenomena are diverse, their essence is a single quiescence;
because of *prajñā*, although it is the one true reality of non-duality, the great function manifests without obstruction.
Commentary on the Vajrasamādhi Sūtra, Scroll Three;
Commentary on the Vajrasamādhi Sūtra, Scroll Four.
Annotated by the Śramaṇa Yuǎnchéng of Xiǎnshèng Monastery in Kuàngzhōu, Huijì County.
The Seventh Chapter: The Tathāgata’s Treasury.
At that time, the householder Brahmacharin rose from his seat and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable One, the meaning of arising is non-extinction, and the meaning of extinction is non-arising. Suchness is precisely the Bodhi of the Buddha; the nature of Bodhi is without discrimination."
Non-conceptual wisdom differentiates the infinite and inexhaustible marks; only when conceptualization is extinguished do such marks of meaning become inconceivable.

Within this inconceivability, there is no conceptualization. Venerable One, as for the fact that the enumerations of all phenomena are immeasurable and boundless, and that the marks of these boundless phenomena are of a single true nature and abide solely in a single nature—how is this so?
The preceding inquiries by Bodhisattvas such as Vimukta manifest the meaning of the Middle Way; the subsequent inquiry by Śāriputra manifests the meaning of True Emptiness.
Herein, the inquiry by the Elder manifests the meaning of the wondrous existence of conventional truth.
This wondrous existence is not [substantial] existence, and this true emptiness is not [absolute] emptiness; both adorn the inconceivable realm of the Dharma-nature. Thus it arises.
The meaning of non-extinction refers to the fact that intrinsic nature is neither arising nor ceasing.
The meaning of non-arising through extinction refers to the fact that arising and ceasing are dependent origination. Thus, there is no arising yet it does not obstruct the blazing manifestation;
there is no extinction yet it does not hinder the quiescent, eternal cessation. This is the Middle Way of the Buddha’s Bodhi for the sake of liberating sentient beings.
When expressed through the manifestation of written words, such a discussion is conducted as follows:
If the self-nature of ultimate bodhi is such that it cannot be differentiated, then the ordinary person’s conceptualization of that which is non-conceptual is called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*).
When the Buddhas, at the time of differentiation, realize the meaning of non-differentiation, this is called "wisdom" (*jñāna*). Why is it called wisdom? Because it is one.
All phenomena arise from conceptual discrimination; because they are realized as non-arising, they are said to possess the characteristic of being inexhaustible.

Only when discrimination ceases does this meaning manifest: arising and non-arising, cessation and non-cessation, discrimination and non-discrimination—all are ungraspable and beyond the reach of thought.
Because they are inconceivable, they are manifested in accordance with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
When a strong man extends his arm, where else could there be room for further discrimination?
Because there is no discrimination, he fully encompasses the infinite and boundless Buddha-dharmas. "I abide solely in one nature"—what is the meaning of this?
It refers back to the previous point that all Buddha-dharmas abide within a single four-line verse.
The Buddha said: "O Householder, it is inconceivable. I have taught all dharmas for the sake of those who are deluded and as a skillful means to guide them.
The characteristics of all dharmas are the wisdom of the single true meaning. Why is this? It is like a marketplace with four great gates;
though one enters through any of these four gates, all lead back to the same marketplace. Likewise, the various flavors of the Dharma are entered according to the inclinations of the multitude."
It is likewise so.
The Buddha said: "That you are able to constantly maintain this single nature is inconceivable. Why is this?

It is because the *tathatā* (true thusness) of sentient beings does not maintain its own nature, but manifests in accordance with conditions; they remain profoundly unaware of this and desire to return to it."
