Because they are deluded, their minds are guided through various skillful means;
although these various skillful means are taught, that to which they ultimately lead is none other than the single true meaning. It is like a single marketplace with four gates:
those who enter through the four gates reach nothing but that same marketplace, for while the paths from the east, west, south, and north differ, each leads conveniently to its destination.
Although one attains the fourfold non-duality, the places reached cannot but be manifold. Why? Because there are no two distinct locations.
Since the faculties of all sentient beings—whether sharp or dull, partial or complete—are not uniform, the teachings spoken must necessarily differ accordingly.
Yet, in the ultimate sense, that to which they all return is but a single self-nature; because this nature is non-dual, one is thus able to abide in this single nature.
This is inconceivable. The Elder Brahmacharin said:
"If the Dharma is thus, I abide in a single flavor (ekarasa) that should encompass all flavors. The Buddha said:
"It is so, it is so. Why? Because the true meaning of the single flavor is like a great ocean into which all streams flow."
There is nothing that does not enter into the flavor of all dharmas possessed by the Elder;

just as those various streams differ in name and number yet their water is no different, so too, when one dwells in the great ocean, all streams are encompassed, and when one dwells in the single flavor, all flavors are subsumed.
When one opens the four gates at the front of the marketplace, one knows that abiding in the single flavor (ekarasa) inherently encompasses all flavors;
the Buddha’s seal approves this and further expands upon the analogy: the single flavor is like the great ocean, and the manifold flavors are like the hundred rivers.
It is one within the many, and many within the one—perfectly interfused and sovereign. The ocean does not say, "I am able to contain the hundred rivers within me."
The rivers also do not say, "We are returning together to the great ocean, without coming or going.
This is the meaning of the passage above, which uses a metaphor to clarify the Dharma; the following section applies the Dharma to the metaphor, and the text is clear and easy to understand.
The Elder Brahmacārin said, "If all dharmas are of one flavor, why is it that the paths of the three vehicles differ, and their wisdoms are distinct? The Buddha said, "Elder, it is like this:
for example, the rivers, streams, seas, and marshes differ in size; they differ in depth; they differ in name and designation.
Water in a river is called 'river water'; water in the Huai River is called 'Huai water'; and water in the Yangtze River is called 'Yangtze water.'"

Just as river waters, though distinct in name, are called only "ocean water" once they are within the sea, so too is the Dharma: when both are within True Suchness (tathatā), they are called only the "Buddha-way.
When a householder dwells in this single Buddha-way, he immediately masters the three practices.
The nature of the mind is one and the same; the differences in the capacities of ordinary beings—whether great or small—are like the waters of rivers and streams.

The size of the water serves as a metaphor for the capacity of the mind-nature. True Suchness does not abide in its own nature and receives names according to its manifestations, just as water has no fixed name.
When water is in a river, it is called "river-water"; this functional application serves as a metaphor for the mind-nature abiding in ordinary beings.
Those called "ordinary beings" exist within the state of the holy, while those called "holy" are vast and expansive. To illustrate by analogy:

the six realms and four modes of birth are infinite in their varieties, yet there is none that does not arise from the single nature. If one can comprehend this nature and return to its source, all is unified within the single Buddha-nature.
Because there is but a single nature, one who abides in this principle of oneness will immediately realize the three practices.
The Elder Brahmācārin asked, "What are the three modes of practice? The Buddha said, "First, the mode of practice that grasps according to phenomena;

second, the mode of practice that grasps according to consciousness; and third, the mode of practice that grasps according to suchness. The Elder said, "In this way, these three modes of practice encompass all gateways; there are no gateways of all dharmas that do not enter into them.
One who enters by means of these practices does not give rise to the mark of emptiness. One who enters in this manner may be said to have entered into suchness."
Regarding the *ālayavijñāna* entering the *tathāgatagarbha*, it is because of both entering and not entering.

For those who grasp according to phenomena, True Suchness does not maintain its own nature but manifests in accordance with conditions; this is the meaning of conventional truth as illusory existence.
For those who grasp according to consciousness, True Suchness does not destroy its own nature but remains unchanging while following conditions.

Just as the practitioner who grasps [the truth], the meaning of the inconceivable Middle Way—the non-duality of the ultimate and the conventional—is such that all mundane and supramundane phenomena are exhaustively subsumed within these three wondrous gates of emptiness, provisionality, and the middle, without exception.
Entering these three gates, one does not give rise to the notion of emptiness, nor the notion of non-emptiness, nor even the notion of both emptiness and non-emptiness; this is the Three Truths.
"Perfectly merging into that which is neither entering nor non-entering, yet entering—that mastery of negation and illumination is the meaning of the *tathāgatagarbha*.
This passage from the sutra briefly sets forth the terminology: namely, the empty *tathāgatagarbha*, the non-empty *tathāgatagarbha*, and the empty-and-non-empty *tathāgatagarbha*.
As for what is called "entering," it means that the practitioner does not give rise to the mark of emptiness; it does not exclusively clarify the One True [Dharma-realm].
This can be clearly understood.
The Elder Brahmācara said: "The inconceivable entry into the Tathāgatagarbha is like a sprout becoming a fruit; there is no place of entry.
When the fundamental root’s sharp power has been sharpened and perfected, one attains the original and attains the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*). How great is that wisdom?"
What is called the *tathāgatagarbha* is the intrinsic nature that is primordially complete and not acquired through cultivation.
Because sentient beings are deluded regarding this inherent [nature], the Buddha employs skillful means to subdue them, causing them to turn back from delusion and attain awakening;

thus he speaks of "cultivation" and "the manifestation of clarity when defilements are exhausted. This is the natural law (*dharmatā*) of the *tathāgata*. How could it come from without? Since it does not come from without, [it is not something newly produced].
If one practices cultivation, one naturally attains the Way; it is like a crop ripening into fruit—not expected, yet it happens, and one does not know why it happens, nor how it happens.
Indeed, the fruit does not exist apart from the crop; if one obtains the method of weeding, the crop will ripen into fruit, but if one does not obtain the method, the fruit will not form.
The fruit of the Way for sentient beings is also like this. If...
If one knows the correct path of cultivation, one may hope for its attainment; if one does not know the correct path of cultivation, one will not accomplish the Way.
Since the Way can indeed be accomplished, at the time of attaining it, how much wisdom will be gained?
The Buddha said: "His wisdom is inexhaustible; to speak briefly, his wisdom is fourfold. What are these four? First is the wisdom of concentration, which refers to conforming to suchness (*tathatā*).
Second is the wisdom of non-concentration, which refers to the skillful means (*upāya*) that crush and destroy [afflictions].

Third is the wisdom of nirvāṇa, which refers to the lightning-like awakening through the elimination of ignorance by means of insight (*prajñā*). Fourth is ultimate wisdom, which refers to entering reality and being fully endowed with the Path."
The Elder has thus employed these four great matters as taught by the Buddhas of the past: they are a great bridge and a great ford for crossing over.
If one intends to transform sentient beings, one should employ this wisdom; the Elder employs these as his great functions. Furthermore, there are three other great matters:
first, within the three samādhis, the internal and external do not obstruct one another; second, regarding the categories of the Great Meaning, one follows the Path.

Regarding the three types of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*): through wisdom as it is, meditative concentration as it is, and compassion conjoined with benefit—by accomplishing these three matters, one attains *bodhi*.
If one does not practice these matters, one will not flow into that ocean of the four wisdoms and will allow the great Māras to find an opportunity.
Elder, you and the great assembly should constantly cultivate this until the attainment of *buddhahood*, never allowing it to be lost for even a moment. (Brahmin)
The Householder said, "What are the three samādhis? The Buddha said, "The three samādhis are namely:

the emptiness samādhi (*śūnyatā-samādhi*), the signless samādhi (*animitta-samādhi*), and the wishless samādhi (*apraṇihita-samādhi*). Regarding these samādhis, Householder, what is the 'Great Meaning' (*mahārtha*) and the 'Classification' (*vibhāga*)?

The Buddha said, "'Great' refers to the four great elements (*mahābhūta*); 'Meaning' refers to the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*); and 'Classification' refers to the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*)."
Regarding the section on the Great Meaning (*mahārtha*):
those of fixed wisdom are those who previously followed the principle of suchness (*tathatā*) in accordance with the Middle Way;

those of unfixed wisdom are those who previously followed the grasping of phenomena in accordance with specific objects; and those who seek nirvāṇa are those who previously followed the grasping of consciousness in accordance with its objects—all three are empty.
The ultimate wisdom within the provisional is neither emptiness, nor the provisional, nor even the Middle Way;

therefore it is said that the two extremes are entirely non-existent and the Middle Way need not be established. The preceding three practices are the cause and constitute the practice of self-cultivation;
these four wisdoms are the fruit and constitute the virtue of benefiting others. This is because all phenomena converge upon suchness.
Because it does not transcend the [five] destinies, True Suchness is definitive wisdom (*niyata-jñāna*).

Because it transforms and delivers beings through skillful means that are appropriate to their capacities and without fixed method, liberation is non-definitive wisdom (*aniyata-jñāna*). Sentient beings are shrouded by ignorance and entangled by afflictions;
only Prajñā illuminates these delusions, and there is no delusion that is not destroyed. When delusions are destroyed, there is peace and bliss; therefore, Prajñā is called Nirvāṇa-emptiness.
When the three names—provisional, middle, and ultimate—are established together, the name does not correspond to the reality; therefore, it is called "ultimate.
When all three are forgotten, both name and reality are transcended, and the path of speech and thought is severed; this is what is meant by entering reality with full perfection.
These four wisdoms are not something I alone proclaim; every past Buddha has taught them. To know these four is to know the great bridge.

Because all worthy sages of the Liang dynasty ascended together [to this state], and because there are no sentient beings who do not receive universal relief, both the holy and the ordinary alike partake of its benefits.
If you wish to transform sentient beings, there is no other way than this.
Samādhi is called "right view" and is also named "right concentration. Because of right view, various delusions do not arise within; because of right concentration, [the mind remains steadfast].
Not being robbed by external objects is specifically the intention for self-benefit. However, if one were to discuss benefiting others fully:
internally not perceiving a mind that can deliver others is emptiness (*śūnyatā*); externally not perceiving the multitude of beings to be delivered is signlessness (*animitta*).
Since both internal and external are empty, there is no activity in the interval; it is naturally free and not robbed by either the internal or the external. Thus it is great.
This means that the four great elements are the meaning of the physical body; the aggregates, elements, and sense bases are the categories of form and mind.

What was previously called the "fundamental root" refers to its sharpness and power. Taking this fundamental root as the essence, one subsequently examines their sharpness or dullness to select the good and eliminate the evil.
As for how to select and eliminate: for those among the multitudes of the six realms who are solely deluded in mind, [the teaching] is opened.
Because the mind [is the primary focus], the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are taught; for those who are deluded regarding form alone, the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*) are taught;

and for those deluded regarding both form and mind, the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*) are taught. To select and cultivate according to the specific category of one's path is what is called "skillful means" (*upāya-kauśalya*).

Just as a wise person is not obstructed by the illumination of knowledge, they employ skillful means to harmonize with the capacities of sentient beings. Therefore, it is said that "prajñā is without cognition."

Yet there is nothing he does not know, just as one who is in meditative concentration (samādhi) does not arise from the concentration of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) while manifesting all modes of dignified conduct (īryāpatha).
Since he does not arise from the concentration of cessation, his self-benefit is already perfected; since his wisdom-illumination is unimpeded, his benefit for others is abundant.
The elder’s question implies: upon entering the Tathāgatagarbha, how many types of wisdom should be attained? And it is that within the Tathāgatagarbha, four types of wisdom should be attained.

However, these four wisdoms are not something that can be attained through deliberate grasping; one can cultivate these three matters and enter [the path] without intending to do so, yet if one does not cultivate these three, one will not be able to enter.
Because one fails to enter, one is seized by the great Māra.
Therefore, know that these three are not merely for ordinary people or lesser sages who might stop midway; even until the attainment of Buddhahood, one should not cease them for even a moment.
In the commentary on the section on relinquishing, two [of the three] are complete while one is missing; that is to say, by citing two, one knows the three.

The Elder Brahmacharin said: "Such matters of wisdom—benefiting oneself and benefiting others, transcending the stages of the triple world, not abiding in nirvana, and entering the bodhisattva path—are inconceivable.
Such characteristics of phenomena are dharmas of arising and ceasing, for they are distinguished through conceptualization."
Therefore, if one were separated from conceptualization (*vikalpa*), phenomena would not cease.
Thus, the "matter of wisdom" refers to the four aforementioned wisdoms; by means of skillful means (*upāya*), they crush and destroy [obstacles], which is for the benefit of others.

Following this, the wisdom of self-benefit removes the flash of lightning-like awakening; this is spoken of in terms of both self and others. Since the praise of self-benefit is integrated herein, it is transcendent.
Because they transcend the nine stages of the three realms for the sake of benefiting others, they employ skillful means to manifest births and do not abide in nirvana;

this is the Bodhisattva path, which immediately enters the reality of the previously mentioned complete path. If these four wisdoms are interpreted as being four distinct wisdoms, they are then phenomena subject to arising and ceasing because they involve conceptual discrimination.
However, if one realizes that the four wisdoms are without correspondence [to separate entities], their essential nature is non-arising and free from all parts.
"Discriminate thus: the nature of mental phenomena is fundamentally neither arising nor ceasing, because a point of origin cannot be apprehended.
At that time, the Tathāgata, wishing to proclaim this meaning, spoke these verses:

Phenomena arise from conceptual construction; they likewise cease through conceptual construction. To extinguish all phenomena of conceptual construction—this is the Dharma that is neither arising nor ceasing.
Whether wholesome or unwholesome, phenomena are produced by transformation from the mind; as the mind follows after conceptual construction, so do phenomena arise. The nature of phenomena...
That which arises from conceptualization is further peeled away by subtle conceptualization; what is the nature of dharmas?
Because they have no nature, conceptualization does not arise, and dharmas likewise cease accordingly.

When both the mind that conceptualizes and the dharmas being conceptualized are forgotten, the true nature shines alone. Since it is neither arising nor ceasing, the ancients called it "spiritual" (ling).
The light alone shines radiantly, utterly transcending the sense organs and their objects; by merely departing from delusory conditions, one is the Buddha of Suchness.
This concludes the answer to the Elder’s understanding: "I abide in the single flavor, which should encompass all flavors."
At that time, the householder Brahmācārin, having heard these verses, was filled with great joy and, wishing to proclaim their meaning, spoke these verses:
"All phenomena are fundamentally quiescent; Quiescence itself is without arising. Such are all these phenomena of birth and cessation."
This dharma is not non-arising; that [non-arising] is not shared with this.
Because it would entail the extremes of annihilationism or eternalism, this is free from the two. Nor does it abide in oneness.
If one were to say that phenomena possess oneness, this characteristic is like seeing falling hairs, or like the delusion of water in a mirage; because all things are false and illusory.
If one sees that phenomena are non-existent, these phenomena are identical to emptiness. Like a blind person without eyes who perversely speaks of phenomena as being like the hair of a tortoise;
now that I have heard the Buddha’s teaching, I know that phenomena are not a duality of views, nor do I abide in a middle way.
Therefore, from non-abiding, I grasp the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata.
All arise from non-abiding; I come from the place of non-abiding. In this place I pay homage to the Tathāgata;
I reverently bow to the marks of the Tathāgata. Equal to space, the immovable wisdom;
unattached and without location, I reverently bow to the non-abiding body. In all places, I constantly behold all the Tathāgatas.

I only pray that all Tathāgatas will explain for me the eternal Dharma—that which is the Dharma of quiescence refers to the Dharma realized by the Tathāgata; that which is subject to arising and ceasing refers to dharmas produced from delusion.
These are dharmas of false discrimination, [yet they are] the principle of the non-arising of true suchness (tathatā).
True Suchness (Tathatā) is free from the dualistic conceptual attachments of permanence and annihilation, just as water and fire cannot coexist;
it is by their very nature that they are so. The principle of True Suchness not only does not cling to these two extremes, but furthermore does not abide in the middle either.
Being unattached in these three places may be called the Great Way of No-Direction (Amūrdha-mārga). Those non-Buddhists and ordinary worldlings do not understand the reality of True Suchness.
The meaning of "concealment" (or "hiding") is this: regarding all phenomena, one falsely gives rise to discrimination by positing them as either existent or non-existent.

If one says that phenomena exist, one falls into the view of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*). For example, seeing hair-tufts, flames, or water where there is none—how could this not be false and deluded?
This refutes the ordinary person who holds to eternalist views. If one sees phenomena as non-existent, one would be the same as empty space; yet empty space itself has no vision.
"You have neither hearing nor knowledge, nor do you possess discernment; yet you currently possess seeing and hearing—how could this be the same as being sightless?

You currently possess speech—how could this be equal to the hair of a tortoise? This refutes the non-Buddhists who hold to the view of annihilationism. They have been taught by false teachers and thus fall into these two views.
Because I have heard the World-Honored One’s instruction, I am not attached to the three locations. Why am I not attached? It is because of the Dharma.
Because there is no fixed direction, the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma involves no fixed dharma that can be taught.
Since the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma has no fixed self, I have set my mind upon no fixed place. Because of non-abiding, there is nowhere he does not abide;
like space, it pervades the entire Dharma-realm without coming or going. In every particular thing, in every phenomenon, it is manifest before one's very eyes.
"I have previously always seen the Tathāgata.
At that time, the Tathāgata spoke these words: "O sons of good family, listen attentively. For you, this assembly, I shall explain the Dharma of Permanence.
Sons of good family, the Dharma of Permanence is not an impermanent dharma; it is neither speech nor letters, and it is not even truth."

Liberation is neither non-existence nor an objective realm; it transcends all delusions and the limits of annihilation. This Dharma is not impermanent, for it is free from all views of permanence and nihilism.
To perceive consciousness as permanent is to see that this consciousness is eternally quiescent, and even this quiescence is itself quiescent.
Son of good family, one who knows the quiescence of phenomena does not quiesce the mind; the mind is eternally quiescent. One who attains quiescence has a mind that is eternally true.

Contemplating and knowing that all names and forms (nāmarūpa) are merely the deluded mind and the conceptualization of the deluded mind, one realizes that there is no other phenomenon apart from names and forms.
Knowing phenomena thus, one does not follow literal expressions; the mind does not conceptualize meanings as "I" or "mine.
When one knows these are mere provisional names, one immediately attains quiescence (śamatha). Upon attaining quiescence, one attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
You have requested that I speak for you of the eternal Dharma; yet "the eternal" and "the impermanent" are merely verbal designations without substantial reality.
If it were the principle of true eternity, it could not be expressed by words, nor could it be conveyed by characters; it would not be something that could be verified through the [four] truths.
Liberation may be sought; although it is not something consisting of speech and the like, it is nonetheless a real dharma. It is not like the empty and unreal [views] of the non-Buddhists.
Although it is a real dharma, it is fully possessed within one's own mind and is not an external object.
Since it is not the same as an external object, it is not the same as annihilationism or eternalism. Why are they not the same? Because my own mind is truly eternal.
The Dharma is not non-existent, and thus it is not annihilation; it is not existent, and thus it is not permanence.
If one can realize that one’s own mind is truly eternal, then one knows that this mind is the permanence of quiescent extinction (*śānta-nirodha*), not the permanence of mere non-annihilation.

If one were to dogmatically cling to the notion that there is a quiescent extinction to be attained, one would likewise fall into falsehood; such a thing is truly impossible. Since there is no quiescent extinction to be attained, why [is it so]?
If one knows it to be quiescent extinction (*śānta-nirvāṇa*), then while the dharmas known are quiescent, the mind that is able to know them has never been quiescent.
Because the mind is eternally quiescent, there is no need for further knowledge to attain quiescence;

rather, when the mind merges with true contemplation (*bhūta-darśana*), it realizes that the essence of all dharmas, such as name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), is quiescent extinction. It is only through the mind’s conceptual discrimination that one perceives these as existing.
When one does not fully grasp that dharmas are thus, then one knows that all dharmas are neither letters nor words;

because one knows they are not [such], one does not fall into the mind of words and phrases. When the mind accords with the true meaning, one does not cling to either self or non-self, for both are quiescent.
At that time, the elder Brahmācārin, having heard these words, spoke this verse:
"Name, sign, and the discrimination of things, Along with the designation of phenomena—these three;
True Suchness and correct, sublime wisdom— These together constitute the five. I now understand these dharmas, And am released from the bonds of eternalism and nihilism."
Entering the path of arising and ceasing, This is annihilation, not permanence. The Tathāgata teaches the Dharma of emptiness, which is far removed from annihilation and permanence;
Due to conditions, nothing is not born. Because there is no birth, there is no cessation.
To grasp at conditions as being existent Is like picking flowers from the sky, Or like the daughter of a barren woman.
Ultimately unobtainable, it is free from all grasping at causes and conditions; Nor does it cease through another, for its own nature is vast.
Because it relies upon suchness, it attains reality; Therefore, the dharma of true suchness should be sovereign as suchness itself.
All myriad phenomena are not like that which is manifested by consciousness.
Phenomena apart from consciousness are empty; therefore, they are taught from the standpoint of emptiness.

Having extinguished all phenomena of arising and ceasing, one abides in nirvāṇa. Yet, being seized by great compassion, one does not abide in the extinction of nirvāṇa, but rather enters the tathāgatagarbha, wherein the grasped and the grasper have ceased to revolve.
Regarding the various phenomena of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) that arise from the conceptualization of a deluded mind:
all phenomena, whether mundane or supramundane, arise through mutual dependence and are all unreal. Although these phenomena have many names, they do not exceed five categories, namely:
name (*nāman*), appearance (*nimitta*), conceptualization (*vikalpa*), right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), and suchness (*tathatā*). That which transcends both name and word is [the ultimate reality].
To realize that what is called "emptiness" is not an objective realm is to realize that characteristics are empty and thus not ultimate truths;
to realize that deluded thoughts are empty and thus not liberation is to realize that correct wisdom and suchness are empty.

When one opposes correct wisdom to deluded thoughts and suchness to illusory appearances, and thereby gives rise to the realization that the root of the deluded is fundamentally empty, then even "truth" cannot be established. I have heard this before.
Each and every teaching of the non-Buddhists is clung to as being real and existent;
they are bound by the shifting extremes of annihilationism and eternalism, entering into that path of arising and ceasing which is not the true, eternal, and non-arising-non-ceasing Way.

Now, having heard the Tathāgata’s teaching of the ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), one distances oneself from these two interpretations—these two extreme dharmas—and realizes that what arises from causes and conditions is the dharma of true emptiness.

It does not belong to causes and conditions; for by the nature of causes and conditions, phenomena are definitively subject to arising and ceasing. Since true emptiness is non-arising, there is no cessation.
If those non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) cling to the idea that phenomena produced by causes and conditions exist, they fall into the view of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*);

if they cling to the idea that they are definitively non-existent, they fall into the view of nihilism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*). Thus, within such conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) of existence and non-existence, one desires—

When seeking the ultimate reality, it is utterly unattainable; it is like a madman gathering flowers from the sky, or like seeking the birth of a son from a stone woman—it is ultimately impossible to find.

One who thoroughly understands dependent origination realizes that the characteristic of arising does not occur apart from causes and conditions, nor is the characteristic of cessation grasped as something separate from causes and conditions. Thus, the *Madhyamaka* states: "That which is produced by causes and conditions..."

I teach that phenomena are emptiness, yet they are also termed provisional designations and are termed the meaning of the Middle Way. That which has already been explained refers to the meaning of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*);
"aggregates" (*skandha*), "elements" (*dhātu*), and "bases" (*āyatana*) refer to the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). All such things are understood to be entirely unreal;
only by relying upon the true essence of *tathatā* (Suchness) can they be termed real. Therefore, True Suchness is called sovereign over all phenomena.

All phenomena depend upon the transformations of consciousness; apart from consciousness, they do not exist. Because they do not exist apart from consciousness, the Buddha designated them as "true" and spoke of them as "empty.
Speaking of emptiness serves to refute existence. If one refutes existence yet remains attached to emptiness, one is deficient in great compassion.
Only by abandoning both existence and non-existence, neither entering saṃsāra nor abiding in nirvāṇa, and transcending to the Middle Way, can one [truly realize it]. Then...
Both the grasper and the grasped enter the Tathāgatagarbha, because the Tathāgatagarbha is empty of adventitious defilements yet not empty of its own nature.
At that time, when the great assembly heard this teaching, they all attained right livelihood and entered the ocean of the Tathāgata’s Tathāgatagarbha.
Chapter Eight: On Dharani.
At that time, Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva rose from among the assembly, went before the Buddha, joined his palms, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable One, I observe that there are matters of doubt in the minds of the great assembly that have not yet been resolved. Now, the Tathāgata..."
"To remove your doubts, I shall now answer whatever questions you have for the sake of the assembly. May the Buddha, out of his compassion, graciously grant me permission.
The Buddha said, "O Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, that you are thus able to deliver sentient beings is a mark of inconceivable great compassion.
You may ask extensively; I shall explain it for you."
The *Dhāraṇī* (Total Retention) encompasses the meaning of the preceding seven chapters. It can "retain" like the earth and "store" like a treasury;
therefore, it is represented by Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva. Furthermore, it is detached from the subject and severs the object, like the earth's holding of things;

it nurtures and gives birth to the myriad phenomena, like the earth's ability to store. Because the assembly’s doubts were not yet exhausted upon hearing the preceding teaching on non-arising, [this chapter] was subsequently produced.
The question on illumination refers to asking questions on behalf of the assembly to demonstrate that one has no doubts oneself;

the Tathāgata’s profound praise is to certify that one has no doubts oneself while questioning for the sake of the assembly, so that those present may each have self-confidence and not harbor other views.
The Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha said, "How can it be that all phenomena do not arise through conditions? At that time, the Tathāgata, wishing to proclaim this meaning, spoke these verses:
If a phenomenon is produced by conditions, A phenomenon could not exist apart from conditions; How then could the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) be non-existent?

Furthermore, regarding phenomena that can arise, internal consciousness serves as the cause and external objects serve as the condition; moreover, the initial impetus is the cause and the auxiliary support is the condition.

Alternatively, because there is conceptual differentiation based on the mind, the mind is the cause and the object is the condition; or, because conceptual differentiation arises based on the object, [the object is the cause and the mind is the condition].
Specifically, the object serves as the cause and the mind as the condition; these two arise reciprocally, each lacking intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Because they lack intrinsic nature, I say that causes and conditions are non-arising.

If those ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) cling to the existence of causes and conditions that can produce phenomena, since those phenomena arise from conditions, they perish when the conditions disperse. When they perish, all things are revealed [as empty].
If there is absolutely no "non-existence," then who is it that cultivates and realizes the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)?
If the nature of the non-arising of dharmas does not belong to arising and ceasing, how could the causes and conditions of arising and ceasing give rise to this nature of the non-arising of dharmas?
At that time, Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva said: "If dharmas are without arising, how can one speak of dharmas? Dharmas arise from the mind.
Thereupon, the Venerable One spoke this verse:
"The dharmas produced by this mind, These dharmas as the grasped and the grasper, Are like flowers in the sky seen by a drunken eye."
This dharma is naturally not that dharma;
if there were no arising, then there would be no phrases, no letters, no speaking, and no demonstrating.

Taking what was previously stated—that it is neither speech nor letters—as the basis for this objection: if it were not speech, there should be no speaking; if it were not letters, [there should be no letters].
"It should not be that there is anything to be shown; since there is no teaching to be shown, how can one speak of the Dharma? [The interlocutor asks: 'Does the Dharma arise from the mind?

The World-Honored One replied: 'The Dharma is fundamentally without arising. Because all sentient beings are deluded regarding this fundamental non-arising and become attached to subject and object, I say that the phenomena of subject and object, and those produced by them, are all merely false imaginings and are not the original mind. It is just like being intoxicated.'"
The eyes of the deluded perceive empty flowers; now, because the first principle of True Suchness (*tathatā*) taught in this sutra is not the same as the deluded mind, it is said to be "unborn.
Desiring to lead sentient beings to awakening according to their capacities, the previous stage concealed the real and established the provisional, teaching that phenomena arise from the mind;
now, the provisional is discarded and the real is revealed, thus teaching that phenomena are fundamentally non-existent.
This does not contradict their arising.
At that time, Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva said: "If the Dharma is thus, then the Dharma is without dependence.
As for a dharma that is without dependence, the Dharma should be self-established. Thereupon, the Venerable One spoke in verse:
The Dharma is fundamentally neither existent nor non-existent; self and other are likewise so. It has no beginning and no end;
arising and ceasing do not abide.
All dharmas are dharmas that exist in mutual dependence; what is called "dependent origination" is established through conditions. Where there is no dependence, there is nothing to be spoken. Now.
When one contemplates that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is unborn, it should thus be neither dependent nor independent;
if it were independent, then phenomena would exist inherently. However, the fundamental dharma of the supramundane is nameless and signless;
it is beyond speech and beyond letters. It is not only that there is no dependence upon others, but even that it does not establish itself. Why does it not establish itself? The verse answers:

The Dharma is fundamentally non-existent; there is no cause for its existence, yet it is spoken of as existing. The worldly mind perceives the Dharma as fundamentally non-existent; what need is there to wait for its non-existence?
Since existence and non-existence are thus, so too are self and other. This true Dharma has no beginning in the past and no end in the future;
since there is neither beginning nor end, how could there be success or failure? As for the nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*), it is illustrated by analogy with emptiness.
Emptiness is most appropriate because it is empty due to non-arising; thus emptiness does not cease, and the dharma-nature is likewise.
Because emptiness is unestablished, emptiness does not perish, and the dharma-nature is likewise. Such a dharma should be attained through silence;
it may be said to lie beyond thought and reflection. If it falls within the realm of thought and reflection, it is not so.
At that time, Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva said: "The characteristics of all dharmas are themselves primordial nirvāṇa;
the characteristics of nirvāṇa and emptiness are likewise so. There are no such dharmas; these dharmas should be as the Buddha has spoken. There are no such dharmas; these dharmas are thusness."
The teaching of the Three Vehicles speaks of arising and ceasing; the teaching of the One Vehicle speaks of neither arising nor ceasing, which is precisely *nirvāṇa*.
Because *nirvāṇa* is neither born nor extinguished, it is provisionally designated by the name "non-arising and non-ceasing" for the sake of delivering sentient beings.
If one were to grasp this according to its true meaning, then both arising and ceasing and non-arising and non-ceasing are equally unattainable, because they cannot be apprehended.
Because it is attained, it is for the first time called "True Suchness" (*tathatā*); because the Bodhisattva has thus intimately realized it, the Tathāgata seals his understanding as correct.
If there were such a thing as attainment, that too would be false;
because there is no such attainment, it is named "Suchness."
Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva said: "The suchness of suchness is inconceivable; neither common nor uncommon, whether grasped by the mind or grasped as karma, it is entirely empty and quiescent.
Since both the empty and quiescent mind and dharmas are ungraspable, they too should be extinguished in quiescence.
Thereupon, the Venerable One spoke these verses:
All phenomena are empty and quiescent; yet these phenomena are not empty of quiescence. When that mind is not empty, it is realized that the mind does not exist.
It is not "not shared," meaning it does not share in the dharmas of arising and ceasing belonging to the Three Vehicles; nor is it "shared," meaning it is also not something apart from them.

If one thinks that there is a distinct dharma to be attained apart from arising and ceasing, this is not so; the intent is to take the grasper (*grāhaka*) as the act of grasping (*karmagrāha*) and the grasped (*grāhya*) as the object of grasping.
Since both the common and uncommon grasper and grasped ultimately return to emptiness and quiescence, they are inconceivable.
In the verse, the meaning of "inconceivable" is further explained: if dharmas are solely empty and quiescent, then the three vehicles are one.

How can there be superiority or inferiority among those who ride these vehicles? Although this *tathatā* (suchness) and *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) are empty and quiescent, within that emptiness and quiescence they contain the wondrous existence of the non-empty.
Those of the three vehicles are deluded in mind and cling to dharmas; they grasp at emptiness and quiescence as being [merely] empty.
Those of the one vehicle awaken to the mind as non-empty, truly attaining the mind of emptiness; this mind is not [simply] empty.
"It is neither non-empty, nor empty, nor both empty and non-empty;
this is called the inconceivable. At that time, Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva said: "This Dharma is not the three truths; form and mind are empty, and even cessation is extinguished.
When this Dharma was originally extinguished, this Dharma should have been extinguished. Thereupon, the Venerable One spoke these verses:
Phenomena are fundamentally without intrinsic nature; they arise from that [conditionality].
Such is not the case in this context.
Regarding those three truths: form is the conventional truth, emptiness is the ultimate truth, and the mind is the middle way truth. This is what was stated above.
The mind is neither empty nor existent; it resembles the Three Truths. When Bodhisattvas deeply understand that it is neither empty nor existent, this is still a verbal designation.
What is realized in accordance with the nature [of reality] is that the Three Truths are neither quiescent nor extinguished, yet they are said to be extinguished.

Because one takes the dharma to be extinguished and forms a conceptualization of "long-term extinction," this question is asked. The verse answers: "Dharmas without intrinsic nature arise from those [elements of] form and mind."
That which arises from false conditions is now understood to be such that within the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) no such names exist;

where, then, could there be such things as form and mind? Nevertheless, because the nature of phenomena is without arising and there is nothing that does not arise, it manifests in accordance with conditions and is not eternally extinguished.
At that time, Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva said: "All dharmas are without arising and without cessation;
why then do you not speak thus, O Venerable One?

Then he spoke this verse: The abiding place of dharmas has no location; Their characteristics and numbers are non-existent because they are empty. Names and speech are two things distinct from the dharma.

Thus, all phenomena—both the grasped and the grasper—are identical in their origination and cessation from the very beginning; now, by dissolving them through non-origination and non-cessation, they should be equal to empty space.
Why then are they not one? [The interlocutor asks: "Because there are various names. The Buddha replies: "Because they have no abiding place and no intrinsic nature."
That the characteristics and numbers are empty means that their functions are empty. Their essence consists only of names, and their functions consist only of descriptions;
the one who speaks is the function, and that which is spoken of is the essence. Both of these are established through the relationship of subject and object.
Since even these two—subject and object—are established as a pair and do not merge into one, how much less could all phenomena, each possessing its own specific capacity and activity, be conflated?
At that time, Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva said: "The characteristics of all dharmas do not abide on the two shores, nor do they abide in the middle current;
consciousness is also like this. How can various objects of perception arise from consciousness?

If consciousness has the capacity to produce [objects], then that consciousness also arises from [something else]. How can there be non-arising consciousness that is able to produce that which is produced?"

If all phenomena do not abide within the three periods of time, then the object cannot be apprehended; if consciousness does not abide within the three periods of time, then the consciousness cannot be apprehended.
Since both are thus unapprehendable, each lacks its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

If there is no intrinsic nature, yet one says that the object arises from consciousness, it would seem that something is produced; if consciousness has the capacity to produce, it should likewise arise from the object. Since both [possess this capacity],...

How can that which is capable of producing and that which is produced be called non-existent? For what reason is it that the nature of consciousness exists while there is that which produces and that which is produced?
Thereupon, the Venerable One spoke these verses:
"The produced and the producer—these two are the object and the subject of cognition. Both are fundamentally non-existent in themselves."
Grasping at existence is like a flower in the sky or a magical illusion; consciousness arises when there is no [external] object.
Since the object does not exist at that time, it arises only when consciousness is present. At that very moment, consciousness also ceases;
thus, both are fundamentally non-existent, neither being existent nor non-existent. Since there is no arising, consciousness itself is non-existent; how then could an object arise from existence?
Consciousness is fundamentally without arising; that which gives rise and that which is given rise to are both constructed from delusion. Both [subject and object] are originally without substance.

When ordinary beings conceive of them as existing, it is like grasping at flowers in the sky—they can never be obtained. When those of the Two Vehicles conceive of them as non-existent, it is like destroying flowers in the sky—what could possibly be achieved?
To apply the mind in such a manner is likewise called false conceptualization. Why is this so?
If you wish to know whether this is a false imagination, examine it with careful scrutiny: when consciousness has not yet arisen, the object does not exist;
when the object has not yet arisen, consciousness also does not exist. Contemplate the state before mind and object have taken form—where could there be a producer or a produced?
Whether existence or non-existence, all are merely the false conceptualizations of the deluded consciousness. Thus it is.

To deliver sentient beings, it is expediently taught that the nature of consciousness is non-arising; yet, if discussed according to ultimate reality, even non-arising does not exist—how could there be any object?
At that time, Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva said: "The characteristics of dharmas are such that both internal and external are empty; the duality of object and wisdom is fundamentally [non-existent]."
The Dharma of the true mark and true emptiness spoken by the Tathāgata Ajita is not a collection.
"Internal emptiness" means the emptiness of wisdom; "external emptiness" means the emptiness of objects. That which is called "emptiness" is quiescent and unattainable.
If there were an emptiness that could be attained, one would fall back into falsehood; only when quiescence is unattainable is it truly called the Truth.
In truth, all phenomena arise from this [source] and possess no accumulation; thus it is said that "from the root of non-abiding, all dharmas are established.

When a Bodhisattva realizes that the preceding two factors—mind and objects—are not encompassed by the three periods of time, they know that object and wisdom, internal and external, are equal and one.
They are quiescent, quiescent, unborn, and there is nothing that is not so.
He gave rise to an understanding that there is no accumulation;
he presented his realization. The Buddha said, "It is so. This Dharma of suchness is formless and non-abiding; it is neither that which is accumulated nor that which accumulates;
it is neither meaning nor letter. It is a single, fundamental teaching, a profound mass of merit."
Within the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) of true thusness (*tathatā*), not even a single speck of dust is established; how could it interfere with phenomenal forms?
Since form itself does not exist, what locus or dwelling place could there be? As such places do not exist, the accumulation of subject and object completely vanishes. Why does it vanish?
Because in the teachings of the Hīnayāna, there are both words and meanings, and thus much dispute arises; whereas in the Mahāyāna... [the second fascicle].

The single meaning is emptiness, which is neither meaning nor text; it is solely the non-arising of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), which ultimately does not admit even the slightest trace of name or characteristic.
There is no accumulation of worldly things, yet there is the accumulation of supramundane merit.
Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva said: "Inconceivable! The inconceivable aggregate: (7) the non-arising of the five, (8) the quiescence of the six, (9) the emptiness of signs.
There is no existence, there is no non-existence; there is no non-existence, there is no non-non-existence. Just as the Venerable One has taught, the meaning of the Dharma is entirely empty.
Entering into emptiness, there is no activity, yet one does not lose the various karmas. There is no self, no mine, no agent, no object, and no view of a self in body, internally or externally."
Because all fetters and afflictions are completely stilled, all vows also cease. Such is the principle of contemplation;
wisdom, concentration, and True Suchness (Tathatā)—as the Venerable One has always taught—are truly like the Dharma of emptiness, which is indeed a potent medicine.
The inconceivable is the essence of *tathatā*. The inconceivable accumulation is the function of *tathatā*.
As for the essence possessing inconceivable perfuming: when sentient beings are perfumed by ignorance, they become afflicted;
when sages and worthies are perfumed by hearing and reflection, they achieve liberation. Because *tathatā* possesses inconceivable transformation, sentient beings...
The name "accumulation of afflictions" refers to ordinary beings, while "accumulation of merit" is the designation of the noble ones. The scriptural passage appears to be a corruption.

The five consciousnesses and the eighth consciousness are both subsumed under direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). The six consciousnesses and the seventh consciousness are both subsumed under inference (*anumāna*) and conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) phenomena.
Since conditioned phenomena possess arising and ceasing, one should say that the sixth and seventh [consciousnesses] do not arise; the unconditioned has no going.

The response should be as follows: "Regarding the five and eight [consciousnesses] as causes of quiescence: the first eight consciousnesses consist partly of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and partly of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), all equally relying upon the ninth consciousness as their fundamental basis. If those two [aspects] were not present, then the ninth consciousness would also be empty.
Why? Because emptiness is merely expressed through words and characters. Both 'emptiness' and 'non-emptiness' belong to the realm of verbal expression. If one says:

When the path of thought is severed, both existence and non-existence are unattainable. The Bodhisattva skillfully realizes that the nature of words is empty and enters the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
Within this emptiness, there is the meaning of non-emptiness; because there is no practice, there is nothing that is not practiced.
Because there is nothing that is not practiced, one does not lose any karmic actions. By entering the emptiness of the ultimate truth, one is able to perceive the object of perception.

Seeing that the inner and outer fetters of "self" and "what belongs to self" are entirely stilled, and being thus detached from both internal and external, the mind ceases its攀缘 (pān-yuan, objective clinging) and all vows have come to rest.
Wisdom is the essence of the nature and concentration is the function of the nature; these two are unified within the single True Suchness.
The World-Honored One has constantly taught that this single thought-moment of inconceivable contemplation fully possesses these three dharmas.
Thus, regarding these dharmas of emptiness, one previously harbored doubts and could not believe them with clarity; today, reflecting deeply, one realizes they are truly a wholesome medicine.
The Buddha said: "It is so. Why? Because the nature of dharmas is empty, and because emptiness is non-arising, the mind is eternally non-arising and empty."
The nature of non-extinction is the mind of constant non-extinction; emptiness is the mind of non-abiding, and emptiness is also the non-abiding of the mind.

Emptiness is unconditioned, and the mind is likewise unconditioned; emptiness has no entering or exiting, being free from all gain and loss. The aggregates, elements, and sense bases are all likewise non-existent. Just as the mind does not cling, so it is with everything else.
O Bodhisattva, I speak of all these emptinesses for the purpose of destroying all forms of existence.
The seal of approval regarding the dharma of emptiness is the resolution of the "excellent medicine. Below, it explains why the dharma of emptiness is considered an excellent medicine:
because the nature of dharmas (*dharmatā*) is empty. That which is called the "nature of dharmas" refers to their functional capacity (*śakti*).
Because all dharmas possess this capacity, not even for a single moment can a characteristic of arising be found, nor can a characteristic of cessation be found for even a single moment.
Although neither arising nor ceasing can be apprehended, one is nevertheless able to accord with arising and ceasing to establish them;

this is like empty space, whose essence is not the manifold forms yet does not obstruct the manifestation of the myriad phenomena. Therefore, if you wish to know the emptiness of the *dharmatā*, you should contemplate the emptiness of the mind.
The mind is the master of nature, and nature is the capacity of the mind. Capacity is precisely function, and the master is precisely [the master].
The essence and its function are non-dual and equalized within one true emptiness. Why is it that the nature and function are empty?

It is because the characteristics of all phenomena—whether mundane or supramundane, including the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense bases (*āyatana*)—do not exist. Therefore, while the function is always empty, the mind has nothing to which it can cling.
Because there is no clinging, it is identical to that essential emptiness; by realizing this essential emptiness, one no longer remains within the three [realms].
Because it is bound to the realms (*dhātu*), it is a fine medicine. Thus, that which I call emptiness is truly the phrase for "medicine and illness";

when the illness is gone, the medicine is removed, and only then is one called wise. If the illness is gone yet one continues to take the medicine, the medicine conversely becomes an illness—is this not madness?
When I speak of various forms of emptiness, it is for the purpose of destroying existence (*bhāva*); once existence is destroyed, emptiness itself must likewise be abandoned.
To abandon attachment while still grasping at emptiness and existence leads to the fallacy of the two vehicles and various non-Buddhists who deny the self.
The Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha said: "O Venerable One, know that existence is not real, like water in a mirage; know that reality is not non-existent, like the nature of fire.
One who contemplates in this way possesses true wisdom."
The mirage on land is fundamentally not water; when thirsty deer gaze upon it, they call it water.

This serves as a metaphor for all phenomena (*dharmas*), which are fundamentally without characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), yet ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are deluded and attached, interpreting them as having real meaning. Fire-nature arises within wood;
it originally has no location or form that can be apprehended, yet once produced by drilling, it is truly able to burn things. This serves as a metaphor for the Truth (*tattva*).
Since the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is fundamentally devoid of location or form, yet its application in response to conditions is never deficient in the slightest, Master Pang said:
"I only wish that you would empty all that exists; be careful not to reify what does not exist.
Is one who can contemplate in this way not indeed wise?
The Buddha said: "It is so. Why is this? Because this person truly contemplates that the single mark of quiescence and its non-existence are equal;
they grasp it through emptiness and cultivate emptiness, and thus do not lose the vision of the Buddha. Because they see the Buddha, they do not follow the three currents.
Within the Mahāyāna, the three paths of liberation are of one essence and lack intrinsic nature. Because they lack intrinsic nature, they are empty; because they are empty, they are non-existent."
Because signs are signless, there is no action; because there is no action, there is no seeking; because there is no seeking, there is no aspiration.
By means of this karma, the mind is purified; because the mind is pure, one sees the Buddha; because one sees the Buddha, one shall be born in the Pure Land.

Thus, through these profound dharmas, the Bodhisattva diligently cultivates wisdom and meditative concentration through the three transformations, and upon their perfect accomplishment, transcends the triple world.
The true observer is one in whom both subject and object are simultaneously stilled, equalized within the single true emptiness. Because it is empty, two aspects are not seen;
there is nothing to be grasped as an object, and all phenomena are empty. This very state, which is all mind, is called the Buddha. "Buddha" means awakening;
because one awakens to one's own mind, all sentient beings—who are deluded and turned away from their own minds—fall into the three realms of existence and undergo birth and death in vain.
One who is able to awaken to their own mind turns against the current of the three realms of existence and enters the holy stream of the Mahāyāna.
The nature of the path of the Mahāyāna is but a single essence; because its realization has three gates, it is called the three doors of liberation.

The signless (*animitta*) is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); because the Dharma-body is signless, the wishless (*apraṇihita*) is liberation. Although it shatters the sands of phenomena, it is not obstructed.

The essence of the transformative path is solely non-action and non-seeking; it is also called "wishlessness" (apraṇihita). This means that the wisdom of prajñā is fully present within, requiring no external seeking.
Therefore, sentient beings defile their own minds with greed, anger, and ignorance, following the flow of the three realms of existence (trisaṃsāra);
whereas sages and worthies adorn their own minds with emptiness, provisional existence, and the Middle Way, entering the flow of the holy path. To see the Buddha is to see what is correct.

Rebirth in the Pure Land refers to the *niśraya-vipāka* (retributive environment); whether it be the primary body (*svabhāva-kāya*) or the environment (*niśraya*), neither exists apart from one's own mind.

Regarding the three transformations, these are the three gates of transformation—emptiness, the provisional, and the middle—if one practices them diligently without weariness, one will be fully equipped for both self-benefit and the benefit of others.
Wisdom is *prajñā*, concentration is *vimukti* (liberation), and perfect fulfillment is the *dharmakāya*; thus, the three virtues are complete.
"Why is it that you do not transcend the three realms?
Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva replied, "That which the Tathāgata has taught as neither arising nor ceasing is precisely the cessation of impermanence; this is the cessation of arising and ceasing.
Once arising and ceasing have ceased, quiescent extinction is established as permanence. Because it is permanent, it is uninterrupted; it is the uninterrupted Dharma, free from all three [realms]."
Regarding the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) as unstable and like a pit of fire, by relying on what dharma does one reprove oneself and enter through that single gate?

Since "non-arising and non-ceasing" is taught in opposition to arising and ceasing, why is it not true quiescence (*śānti*) because there is something opposed to it? [Answer: Because it is a relative negation (*pratiṣedha*).

The teaching of arising and ceasing as non-arising and non-ceasing was a provisional means of former times. Now, observing the Dharma-nature of the One Vehicle, there is fundamentally no arising or ceasing;

why then should one seek further cessation? If one gives rise to thoughts or mental movements, one merely attempts to extinguish that arising and ceasing, only to realize that such an effort is itself empty and illusory.
If not a single thought arises, the boundaries of past and future are severed; when arising and ceasing do not arise, this is called the True Constant. Because it is constant, it does not cease.

Not obstructed by the three realms—whether moving or unmoving—one directly accords with the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Looking back at conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), one regards them as being equal to a pit of fire.
Thus, all that is seen, heard, known, or perceived, and all names and marks, are termed "conditioned.
If one departs from those conditioned things, there is nowhere for the mind to function; yet if one remains attached to those conditioned things, one falls once again into delusion.
Not knowing upon what dharma to rely for self-reproach regarding names and marks, and not knowing upon what dharma to rely to enter the single gate, the Buddha said:
"A Bodhisattva reproaches his mind through three great matters and enters into practice through three great truths. Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva asked:
"What are the three matters by which one reproaches the mind? What are the three truths by which one enters the single [gate]?"
Regarding the three great matters spoken of by the Buddha: first is cause, second is fruit, and third is consciousness.
These three matters are empty from the beginning; they are not my true self, nor am I their true self. How could I give rise to attachment and defilement toward them?
Contemplating these three matters as being bound by fetters and drifting in the sea of suffering, one should constantly reproach oneself for such things. As for the Three Truths, the first is...
That is to say: first, the path to enlightenment is the truth of equality, not the truth of inequality;

second, it is the truth attained through the right wisdom of great awakening, not the truth attained through false wisdom; third, it is the truth entered through the non-dual practice of wisdom and concentration, not the truth entered by departing from such practice.
One who cultivates the Buddha-way through these three truths will, regarding this Dharma, inevitably attain right awakening.
The stream of the wisdom of perfect enlightenment flows with the Great Ultimate Compassion that benefits both self and others, leading to the attainment of Buddhahood and Bodhi.
Ignorance is the cause and formations are the result; birth, old age, sickness, and death are the results, while consciousness is the sovereign that governs the three periods of time.
Of these, two branches of the past serve as the cause, five branches of the present serve as the result, and three branches of the present serve as the cause.
The two future branches constitute the fruit; the nature of consciousness has no substance because ignorance fails to awaken and falsely gives rise to discrimination.

This is the error of birth and death having no source, and the fault of the conscious mind falsely grasping. If one can deeply contemplate the afflictions of ignorance, then the conscious mind will not arise.
If consciousness does not arise, then birth, old age, sickness, and death are inherently quiescent in their very essence.

However, if this is so, then all transmigration through the three realms is due to these three matters. Because the minds of ordinary beings are coarse, they cannot observe subtly and thus falsely cling to things as being existent;
yet when observed with subtlety, they are fundamentally empty and not real. One falsely clings to them as "self," but how could they be a true self?
Once one realizes that what is not-self is indeed not-self, what attachment or defilement could there be? Therefore, one should...
Deep contemplation reveals that all who are bound by karma and漂流 (drift) in the ocean of suffering do so without exception because of these three matters. At first, one must believe this;

though the power of the Way cannot yet overcome habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), one must repeatedly reproach oneself until there is nothing further to reproach, and thus one will naturally emerge from the triple world (*tridhātu*). As for the path of Bodhi, it is equal.

Because all classes of sentient beings are equal in their capacity to realize the Dharmakāya, Great Awakening is that which is attained through right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*), not through false knowledge (*mithyā-jñāna*).
This refers to the Prajñāpāramitā’s exhortation to select one's teachers and friends; for the harm caused by the false obstructing the right is profound.
That wisdom and meditative concentration are non-different is liberation (*vimukti*); though the Brahma-faring (*brahmacarya*) is manifold, it does not exceed this.
Because they transcend these two, it is said that the Dharma attained by all Buddhas is adorned by the power of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).

Those who are able to cultivate concentration and wisdom possess right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*); those who cannot cultivate concentration and wisdom, engaging only in empty talk on profound principles without actual practice, are collectively termed those with false knowledge (*mithyā-jñāna*).
Such maladies are prevalent in the world—how can one not be cautious? One should be able to reproach oneself through three matters and cultivate the three truths (*trīṇi satyāni*) for oneself.
Having transformed the flow of the three realms of existence into the flow of the wisdom of perfect enlightenment, one’s own benefit is already sufficient;

yet, if one does not arouse compassion to rescue sentient beings, it is as if one lacks a necessary component. One must surely bring about the mutual benefit of both self and others before attaining Buddhahood.

Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva said: "Venerable One, if such a dharma is without causes and conditions, and if a causal dharma does not arise in the absence of conditions, how can the immovable dharma enter the Tathāgata?"
If one understands the meaning that the three matters are fundamentally empty, then if these three matters are fundamentally empty, this Dharma does not belong to causes and conditions.
If it does not belong to causes and conditions, its essence is inherently tranquil. Why, then, do you speak of there being those who enter the Truths and those who do not?
If there were those who enter and those who do not, one could not be called a Tathāgata; yet, if one is named a Tathāgata, then...
There should be no entry [into anything], for the Bodhisattva raised this question out of fear that people might conceive the notion of attainment.
At that time, the Tathāgata, wishing to proclaim this meaning, spoke these verses:
The characteristics of all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature and immovable.
These phenomena do not arise at this time, nor do they arise at any other time. There is no difference in time for phenomena; they do not arise at a different time.
Because their nature is empty, they are quiescent. At the time when their nature is empty and quiescent, [they are thus].

This dharma manifests at this time; because it is free from characteristics, it abides in tranquility. Because it abides in tranquility, it does not take these various dependently arisen dharmas as objects.
This dharma is not produced by conditions; though arising and ceasing through causes and conditions, its nature is without arising or ceasing, empty and quiescent.
The nature of conditions consists of the object and the subject of cognition; these conditions are fundamentally dependent origination.
Therefore, phenomena do not arise from conditions; likewise, there is no arising where conditions are absent.

Phenomena produced by causes and conditions—those very phenomena are themselves the causes and conditions. The characteristic of arising and ceasing within causes and conditions is itself without arising or ceasing;
that is the mark of reality. Fundamentally, there is no coming forth or passing away; such is the state of all phenomena at this time.
Arising spontaneously from emergence and disappearance, it is therefore the ultimate pure source. This source does not depend on the power of the multitude;
rather, within the state subsequently attained, one attains what was originally attained.
All dharmas are thus designated as the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*). If one contemplates by means of their characteristics, then each and every dharma is distinct and manifest.
If one contemplates by means of intrinsic nature, then every phenomenon is empty and quiescent; because they are empty and quiescent, they do not belong to the three periods of time.
Since phenomena do not arise at this [present] time, they are profoundly still and ungraspable in their own place; therefore, there is no "different time.
Because they do not belong to the two extremes, they do not arise at a "different time"; because the prior and posterior limits are severed, they are neither prior, nor posterior, nor intermediate.
When one realizes that the essence is empty and still, how can there be movement or non-movement? From the root of non-abiding, all dharmas are established;
at the time of this unconditioned quiescence, there is nothing that is not done. All phenomena manifest with brilliant clarity, like the myriad stars appearing within the void.
The void has no mind capable of manifesting images, nor does it have any thought toward what is manifested.

Each is without mind and each is without conditions; this is the condition of quiescent extinction (*śānta-nirodha*). Because it is quiescently extinguished, it does not obstruct the manifestation of responses according to conditions.
Ultimately, its essence is fundamentally unborn. Why is this? Because those causes and conditions arise and perish through their own characteristics, yet each lacks self-nature (*svabhāva*);
there is only the single emptiness of nature (*ekalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*) that encompasses them all, leaving no condition unexhausted.
Arising occurs by means of causes and arises by depending on conditions; its establishment is inherently possessed of both the agent and the object, all of which depend upon causes and conditions.

When conditions are absent, the nature of arising also ceases. This further explains the meaning stated above. Why is it said that when conditions are absent, the nature of arising also ceases? The explanation is:

phenomena produced by causes and conditions are themselves the totality of those conditions; they arise and cease as a whole, and this arising and ceasing is the very nature of those causes and conditions. That is the nature of those phenomena.
That which is fundamentally neither arising nor ceasing refers to those phenomena produced from causes and conditions. These phenomena arise from their own causes and conditions;
how could they interfere with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*)? Since the nature of phenomena is without arising or ceasing, it is said that they themselves are without arising or ceasing.
Why are they without arising and ceasing? The commentary states: "The nature of phenomena is another name for True Suchness (*tathatā*). Indeed.
Since the nature of the true suchness (tathatā) and the ultimate reality (bhūtalakṣaṇa) is neither internal nor external, how could there be any entering or exiting?
Nevertheless, all those phenomena take true suchness as their substance, yet they arise and perish of their own accord.

Because one realizes that this arising and perishing is the very substance of non-arising and non-perishing, the dharma-nature is the fundamentally pure essence of true suchness; it stands alone as the illuminating substance, independent and not relying on anything else.
This condition is not an object attained by ordinary beings at their initial stage; rather, it is that which the sages and worthies attain through gradual cultivation across the stages—

from the ten faiths, the ten abidings, the ten practices, and the ten transferences— up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment, where they ascend to wondrous enlightenment and realize their original attainment.
At that time, when Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva heard what the Buddha had spoken, his heart was filled with joy;
and as none among the assembly harbored any doubt, he, having understood the minds of the multitude, spoke these verses:
I know the doubts in the minds of the assembly, which is why I have asked with such earnest persistence.
The Tathāgata, in his great kindness and compassion, has distinguished everything without exception. All these two assemblies have now attained complete clarity.
Now that I have reached this state of understanding, I shall universally transform all sentient beings, just like the Great Compassion of the Buddha.
Not abandoning his original vow, he dwells upon the stage of the "only son" amidst the afflictions.
When the Bodhisattvas, having doubts regarding the causes [of this], raised questions, and when the Lord knew their doubts had been stilled, he spoke these verses.

It may be said that he was the embodiment of great compassion, never establishing a self; yet the World-Honored One, out of his great compassion, extensively [taught] in accordance with what was asked.
He discerns so that the assembly gathered there may all attain clarity; yet, though they have attained clarity, they achieve only their own benefit and not the benefit of others.
Therefore, he exhorts them again to practice the conduct of great compassion to universally benefit all sentient beings, never abandoning their original vows.
Because parents also suffer when their child is ill, [the Bodhisattva] regards all sentient beings as his only son, and thus remains constantly amidst the afflictions.
At that time, the Tathāgata addressed the assembly, saying: "This bodhisattva is inconceivable; he constantly uproots the suffering of sentient beings through great compassion.

If there are sentient beings who uphold this sūtra-dharma or uphold the name of this bodhisattva, they shall not fall into the evil realms, and all obstacles and difficulties will be completely extinguished. If there are sentient beings who uphold this sūtra..."
Abandoning all other discursive thoughts, focus your mindfulness exclusively on this sutra and practice according to the Dharma.

At that time, the Bodhisattva will constantly manifest transformation bodies to preach the Dharma for you, protecting you and never abandoning you for even a moment, so that you may swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
You Bodhisattvas, when transforming sentient beings, must cause them all to practice in this manner.
The definitive meaning of the Mahāyāna is stated in verse:

"Without abandoning their original vows, the bodhisattvas vow that they shall only realize the stage of Bodhi once all sentient beings have been delivered, and they shall never become Buddhas until hell is emptied. This is because their vow is inconceivable compassion.

It is inconceivable that one should not know how to repay the kindness of those who have pulled sentient beings from suffering; yet sentient beings must certainly know how to repay their debt of gratitude.
If one wishes to repay this kindness, there is no other way than to uphold this sutra or to uphold the names of the Bodhisattvas.

Not only will one thus recognize and repay their benevolence and honor the source of one's being, but one will also extensively attain self-benefit, avoid falling into the evil realms, extinguish obstacles, and eliminate transgressions. This is the power of this sutra.
There are two [aspects]: first, the samādhi of upholding the words and letters, by which one attains the inconceivable transformative influence of the Mahāyāna and gains benefits as described above;

second, the realization that the true mark (dharmatā) manifests before one’s own mind in every thought-moment, vividly and without delusion, whereby one gains benefits as described above—this being the natural order of things (*dharmatā*) and not a forced assertion. Therefore, one should cultivate this for the sake of transforming sentient beings.
To teach the Dharma with one’s own body and never abandon it for even a moment until the attainment of Bodhi is the summary praise of constantly uprooting suffering through great compassion.
You present Bodhisattvas have two conditions: first, you should study the great compassion and universal protection of the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha;
second, you should constantly teach sentient beings to practice and cultivate such scriptures as these.
At that time, Ānanda rose from his seat, approached the Buddha, and said to him:

"The Tathāgata has spoken of the mass of merit of the Mahāyāna, which definitively severs the fetters and brings about the inconceivable benefit of the realization of non-arising. What is the name of such a sūtra?
By receiving and upholding this sūtra, how much merit is obtained? I pray that the Buddha, out of compassion, will explain this for me."
The Sūtra is divided into three parts; the introductory section (*nidāna*) and the main body (*saddharma*) are now concluded; this is the section on the dissemination (*parīndanā*).
The mass of merit (*puṇyaskandha*) of the Mahāyāna is inconceivable, and its fruit of karmic retribution is likewise inconceivable.
Those who definitively sever the fetters (*saṃyojana*) transform from the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) into a sage (*ārya*). All sentient beings are sealed by ignorance (*avidyā*).
The eye being bound to forms and the ear to sounds, one fails to attain liberation within the cycle of birth and death.

Now, hearing this sutra, one realizes the true mark of the One Vehicle and fully witnesses that all phenomena are non-arising; this is precisely the self-nature of the wondrously luminous original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*).
Although it is thus original enlightenment, because it is sealed and grasped by ignorance and not relinquished, one remains fixedly attached to the three [realms].
