While it takes the cultivation of great incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*) to realize this sūtra through other means, as soon as the Tathāgata proclaims it, it manifests before one’s mind without being attained through gradual cultivation; this is what is called "inconceivable.
What is the name of such a sudden and wondrous Dharma, and what merit does one obtain by receiving and upholding it?
The Buddha said, "Good son, as for the name of this sutra, it is inconceivable; it is that which has been protected and remembered by all Buddhas of the past.
It can lead one into the ocean of the Tathāgata’s omniscience. If there are sentient beings who uphold this sutra, they will have no further longing for any other sutras.
This dharma of the sutra is a dhāraṇī of all dharmas, encompassing the essentials of all sutras."
Among all the dharmas of the various sūtras, this is the fundamental tenet;
as for the name of this sūtra, it is called the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, also called the *Vajrasamādhi*, and also called the *Aparimitārthasiddhi*.

If there are those who receive and uphold this sūtra, they are said to receive and uphold the merits of hundreds of thousands of Buddhas. It is like space, which has no boundaries and is inconceivable.
"I have deliberated on what I entrust to you, and it is none other than these sutras.
To summarize, Ānanda’s praise is truly inconceivable; they do not belong to the three vehicles, for they are protected by the mindfulness of all Buddhas.
While one may obtain only self-benefit by relying upon and practicing the sutras found within the three vehicles,"
As for its fruits, some may attain the fruit of a Śrāvaka, while others may attain the fruit of a Pratyekabuddha;
yet upon hearing and upholding this sutra even once, one is able to enter the ocean of the Tathāgata’s wisdom—is this not truly inconceivable?
This sutra is the power of the samādhi of one's own mind; the appearance of all Buddhas in the world is nothing other than pointing directly to people’s own minds.
Because taking the realization of one's nature as Buddhahood as one's fundamental aspiration, nothing pointed out by the various sutras transcends this;
therefore, to receive and uphold this is to possess the true sutra of one's own nature, such that there is no further longing for other sutras. The mind is the great root of all dhāraṇīs;

the mind is the vast source of the myriad dharmas. The mind is that which is explained (*lakṣya*), and the sutras are that which explains (*lakṣaṇa*); thus, they constitute the relationship between the object and the subject.
Because it unifies all [teachings], this constitutes the root of *dhāraṇī* and the essential core of all sutras.
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* is that which expresses (*vācaka*) immeasurable meanings, while [the Mahāyāna] is that which is expressed (*vācya*).

Whether as the expresser or the expressed, both rely on the power of the *vajrasamādhi* to sever all obstacles regarding phenomena and principles; therefore, it is the central tenet to which all these sutras are bound. This sutra is thus... [all] sutras.
Because it is the Buddha’s fundamental intention, upholding even a single sutra is equal in merit to upholding the names of hundreds of thousands of Buddhas;
this is but a brief analogy, for if one were to provide a comprehensive analogy, it would be as inconceivable as empty space.
Ānanda asked, "What is the practice of the mind? What kind of person upholds this sutra?

The Buddha said, "Good son, one who upholds this sutra is a person whose mind never falls into gain or loss, who constantly cultivates pure conduct (*brahmacarya*), who always delights in a tranquil mind regarding frivolous discourse, and whose mind remains in meditative concentration even when entering a village;
though living at home, he is not attached to the three realms of existence."
In this present life, such a person enjoys five kinds of blessings: first, they are honored and respected by the multitude; second, their life is not cut short by untimely death;
third, they are able to skillfully refute and respond to heterodox arguments; fourth, they delight in delivering sentient beings; and fifth, they are able to enter the Noble Path.
Such a person as this upholds and maintains this sutra.
Regarding "the mind being without gain or loss," the Sixth Patriarch said: "Do not think of good, do not think of evil;
simply proceed in this manner, and naturally the mind will enter the state of non-arising, serene and eternally quiescent. Furthermore, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:

"Because the mind and speech are straightforward, within that state there is forever no trace of crookedness. This treatise concerns the settling of the mind; through it, one naturally attains realization of the essence.

The Dharma-body Buddha is the meaning of upholding and maintaining; it is for the constant practitioner who, having perfected the body through the six perfections and myriad practices, manifests them spontaneously to realize the Reward-body Buddha.
Thus, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "In principle, there must be sudden awakening, whereby [delusions] are eliminated simultaneously with that awakening;
in phenomena, they are gradually removed until, through successive stages, they are exhausted. This refers to one who delights in stillness yet enters the village, remaining tranquil even amidst it.
To cultivate the Ultimate Truth (paramārtha-satya) while moving within the household life without being attached to the three realms of existence is to realize the ultimate within the conventional;

this explains the meaning of cultivating the mundane truth (saṃvṛti-satya) as the practice of pure conduct (brahmacarya). The Middle Way is not explicitly mentioned here because the text is abbreviated.

One who can thus cultivate these three contemplations in a complete and integrated manner will extensively manifest immeasurable merits; to provide a brief summary, five types of delusion are provisionally indicated.
The mind follows after objects; when the mind awakens, objects follow me. Therefore, one is honored by the multitude. Failing to understand one's own mind, one falsely clings to worldly life.
If one can awaken to one's own mind, one will know that kalpas as numerous as dust motes do not perish;
how then could there be any arbitrary heavenly retribution? Failing to understand one's own mind, one seeks the Dharma outside the mind; all such discourse is merely termed "limited."
If one realizes that all things are but one’s own mind, then there are no phenomena external to the mind; one attains unimpeded penetration and is able to analyze and refute heterodox arguments.

Once one’s own mind is clarified, one will naturally delight in delivering sentient beings. Of these four types mentioned above, the first two pertain to self-benefit and the latter two to benefiting others.
Having fully discussed the stage of the causal ground (*hetu-bhūmi*) and how one may enter the Noble Path, we now discuss the virtues of the fruition (*phala-guṇa*).
Ānanda said, "If such a person were to deliver all sentient beings and receive offerings, would they be able to do so?
The Buddha said, "Such a person can act as a great field of merit for sentient beings; they constantly practice great wisdom, manifesting both skillful means and ultimate reality.
They are the Saṃgha of the Four Reliances, who may accept all manner of offerings—even from their own heads, eyes, marrow, and brains—let alone food and clothing."
Yet one cannot receive [the benefits of] such a son of good family; such a person is your spiritual friend and your bridge.
How much more so should ordinary people make offerings?
All fields of merit are inherently possessed by sentient beings; why then are they obscured by ignorance and afflictions?
Being entangled [in afflictions] is like a bright jewel beneath one's clothes or a treasure-trove within a house; because of delusion, one does not enjoy it and is thus like a pauper.
Those who uphold this sutra can show people the jewel in their clothes and point out their treasure-trove;

therefore, they are fields of merit for those of great wisdom. Regarding the four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*), there are two kinds: first, those of the Hīnayāna, and second, [those of the Mahāyāna].
Regarding the four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*) of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna: first, being able to beg for food for the duration of one’s life;
second, being able to dwell among graves or at the foot of trees for the duration of one’s life; third, being able to collect discarded rags for clothing for the duration of one’s life;

fourth, being able to take only decomposed medicine when ill. The four [reliances] of the Mahāyāna are: relying on the Dharma and not on the person; relying on the meaning and not on the words; relying on sūtras of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*)...

Rely on the *neyārtha* (provisional) sūtras rather than [the literal], and rely on wisdom (*jñāna*) rather than consciousness (*vijñāna*). The Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*) is entirely for one's own benefit, whereas the Great Vehicle (*Mahāyāna*) is for the most part the benefit of others;
because it benefits others, even one's head, eyes, marrow, and brain should be offered, as in the case of Ānanda.
Even those who have entered the stream of the noble ones (*ārya-srotas*) should be revered, let alone ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
Ānanda said, "If one receives, upholds, and makes offerings to such a person who possesses this sutra, how much merit will they obtain?

The Buddha said, "If there were another person who took gold and silver filling an entire city and gave it as a gift, it would not equal the merit of receiving and upholding even a single four-line verse of this sutra from such a person.
It is inconceivable, son of good family, that it causes all sentient beings [to attain liberation]."
One who upholds this sutra has their mind constantly in samādhi and does not lose their original mind; should they lose their original mind, they must immediately perform repentance.
The method of repentance is that which brings cooling relief.

To illustrate extensively, even the seven treasures filling as many Ganges-river sands as there are grains of sand would not surpass it; for fear that people might be startled, [the Buddha] provisionally uses the analogy of filling an entire city.
The merit of the four-line verse derived from receiving [this teaching] is far superior to the gift of gold and silver; it is entirely inconceivable.
Why is this so? Because it purely carries one’s own mind, enabling one to obtain the jewel of mental wisdom—a treasure that worldly riches cannot match.
By maintaining this mind, the mind does not lose its concentration, and all karmic afflictions are instantly cooled.
Ānanda said, "Does the repentance for prior offenses not enter into the past? The Buddha said, "It is so. It is like a dark room:

if it encounters a bright lamp, the darkness is immediately extinguished. Son of good family, do not say that the repentance for all prior offenses is merely a verbal expression that enters into the past."

Sin and merit have no inherent nature and no fixed location; when one is deluded, it is as if dwelling in a great dream, but when one awakens, darkness is instantly dispelled—who then would discuss the three periods of time?
Ānanda asked, "What is called repentance? The Buddha said, "Relying on the teachings of this sutra, enter the contemplation of reality."
Upon entering contemplation, all transgressions are completely extinguished; one leaves the evil realms behind and shall be born in a Pure Land, swiftly attaining Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
To "confess" (chàn) is to repent for past faults, and to "regret" (huì) is to vow against future errors; once past faults are extinguished, future errors will not arise.
When one arises from the intermediate state with tranquility, this is itself called the Pure Land. Ānanda, fearing that people might not understand, requested a further clarification.
The Buddha said: "The self-nature of Bodhi is like the luminosity of a mirror; it is buried by dust and grime and thus does not appear.
When the grime is exhausted, the light appears; it does not come from without. Once one enters contemplation, it is not merely that sins are extinguished—it is the Unsurpassed."
"One should always keep in mind the fulfillment of bodhi.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, Ānanda and the assembly of the four groups of followers, including the bodhisattvas, were all greatly rejoiced;
their minds attained certainty, and they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, joyfully putting his words into practice.
Commentary on the Vajrasamādhi Sūtra, Scroll Four (End).
Postscript to the Commentary on the Vajrasamādhi Sūtra:
Those who know use the mind to clarify words; those who do not know use words to clarify the mind. To clarify the mind with words cannot eliminate [delusion].

It is said that one comprehends words through the mind; not only do words vanish, but the mind likewise vanishes. One cannot be said to have comprehended words unless the words vanish, nor can one be said to have comprehended the mind unless the mind vanishes.
Furthermore, it is only upon the ultimate vanishing of words that the vanishing of the mind is attained, and only upon the ultimate vanishing of the mind is one said to have entered the Way.
How could the Great Way be conceived by thought or discussed in words? It is for this reason that words exist.
How could it be that one can think of or discuss this with the mind? Is it not, therefore, beyond words?

The *Vajrasamādhi Sūtra* directly reveals the supreme vehicle and its definitive meaning; furthermore, when Master Yunmen Zhenran applied his "hand-eye" to handle and expound it, its essential purport became even clearer.
This work, which transmits the orthodox lineage of Caodong and interprets the texts, is but a continuation of that tradition.
Furthermore, in the Cao-Dong school, there is the "Treasure Mirror Samādhi," which is another name for the "Vajra Samādhi.
It is the genuine fodder and the daily meal of the masters; if one chews it thoroughly, one knows its flavor and can impart that flavor to others. Those who can respond to the occasion are few.
Layman Zhanze possesses firm roots of faith and clear, perfect wisdom; he is one who knows the flavor and is fit to be a master.

Might this perhaps have captured the Master’s intent?
